data.title: USD/CAD Forecast: Dollar Bulls Defend Key Support After Breakout
data.description:
The U.S. Dollar continues to rally against the Canadian dollar overall, but Thursday saw a little bit of a pullback. At this point, the market is trying to do what it can to find buyers at the 1.43 level again.

USD/CAD

The U.S. dollar initially rallied against the Canadian dollar during the session here on Thursday, but has given back those gains as we continue to see a lot of noisy behavior. After breaking through the psychologically important 1.43 level, the 1.43 level is an area that a lot of people will be watching, as it was a major turning point multiple times in the past as sellers came in.

The interest rate differential continues to favor the United States

That being said, the market breaking above there clears a structural high from a couple of months ago and now starts to see the U.S. dollar dig into this massive area of resistance that extends all the way to 1.45.

The interest rate differential continues to favor the United States, and it will for the foreseeable future, especially considering that the Federal Reserve is likely to raise rates in December while the Bank of Canada is pretty much where they need to be inflation-wise, barring energy. So we'll have to watch that one.

Plus, we also have to keep in mind that Canada just shed jobs while the United States tripled its estimate. So, with all that coming into play, and the fact that you get paid to hold U.S. debt above inflation at this point, it makes quite a bit of sense that this pair continues to be a buy-on-the-dip scenario, and that's exactly how I'm treating it.

I only want to buy this pair and have no interest in owning the Canadian dollar right now, especially considering that oil is starting to slide a bit also. Ultimately, all things are pointing higher over the longer-term here form what I see.

data.title: Ripple Hangovers Are The Worst
data.description:
THE RIPPLE EFFECT

Long before the advent of cryptocurrencies, the term ripple (noun) meant "a small wave or slight movement on a surface, especially water; or a light, spreading sound, emotion, or effect". (Google AI Overview)

Example: Dropping a pebble into a pond of still water creates ripples which flow gently across the pond.

In the 1960s, Ripple was a carbonated, sweet wine produced by E. & J. Gallo Winery. Light carbonation and a variety of fruit flavors spurred its initial acceptance; however, one additional factor greatly added to its popularity. Ripple was very inexpensive. Originally costing $ 1 per bottle, it was often the drink of choice during the "pop wine" era of the 1970s.

Intended as a cheap table wine, its frequent misuse by those who were inclined to overindulge led to serious consequences. Those consequences were similar to those experienced by others who drank too much and are commonly referred to as a hangover.

For those who preferred the popular, cheap drink of choice, the term "hangover" was exchanged for the more descriptive "ripple effect". The movements, however, were not slight and the undulations were anything but gentle. 

RIPPLE

At one time, Ripple (XRP-X)appeared to be a darling child of the cryptocurrency progeny. Deliberate and conscious attention by various personalities and investors, as well as favorable publicity, popularized the lesser-known Ripple, one of Bitcoin's younger brethren.

The benefits translated to outsized price performance.

Between the end of October 2024 and mid-July 2025, the price of Ripple soared from $.50 to a high of $3.65. The more than seven-fold increase in less than nine months amounted to 630%.  The future looked bright, and Ripple was expected to continue outperforming other cryptocurrencies. 

Unfortunately, the $3.65 price is still the high, and price action since then has been steeply downhill. After breaking the $1 mark briefly, then rallying almost 50%, Ripple recently traded at $.89, down more than 75% from its all-time high set sixteen months ago. 

The hangover must be quite awful for Ripple investors and enthusiasts, and the possibilities for dealing with it are harsh. 

Short-term: 1) Stop consuming (buying) large quantities of cheap wine (Ripple). 2) Don't expect a rapid recovery. 3) Expect the hangover symptoms to worsen. 

Long-term: 1) See number 1 above. 2) Expect a long and winding road, and lower prices before price stabilization occurs. 3) Get lots of rest. You are going to need it. 

Other cryptocurrencies are exhibiting weakness and vulnerability, much as they have since summer 2025. Bitcoin (BTC.X) is the lead dog in the crypto markets, but Ripple is leading the way down in price.

data.title: Why Fast Market Declines May Be Less Concerning Than Slow Bear Markets
data.description:
I think we can call what is going on in markets a fast decline. While this is not fun, market history tells us that slower declines have tended to be more problematic. Look at how slowly the market rolled over from the internet bubble and at the start of the Financial Crisis. Now think about the end of 2018, the Covid Crash and the Tariff Panic. They fell hard and fast and snapped back quickly. Down 6% in a month seems closer to being a fast decline. From my time at Fisher Investments and an indicator I have cited before, to the extent bear markets start slowly, look for an average 2% decline for three months in a row. Anything could happen from here, of course, but for now, this seems fast.

The above chart is a great example of why you diversify your diversifiers. Clients own all of those except for TAIL, and actually, for gold I use GLDM.

BTAL and CAOS are generally working. CAOS responds a little better to declines that are even faster than the current one, but up a little is OK. Managed futures tend to do better with longer, slower declines than where we are at this point. They could be doing well now as a matter of luck, like during the COVID crash, so I am optimistic that they would start to become additive if this in fact does become a more serious event. Gold has had long runs where it has struggled, and lately there has been a short run where it has been struggling.

I've pounded the table on diversifying your diversifiers probably to the point of being boring, but right now is exactly why. Occasionally they'll all work, but expecting that is not realistic. The chart is exactly why I've said I think 25% in gold is a terrible idea. I'm obviously a big believer in managed futures and while we do some interesting theoretical stuff with managed futures here, I keep the allocation in real life pretty small, mid-single digits for the most part.

Some days my mix of diversifiers works very well and we're down a lot less, and some days they are less effective. There's no way to know what will work best in the next market event or to what magnitude they will work, but I think they help more often than not. To the extent they are working, times like now are why you hold on while markets are doing well. There is no way to know when the market will turn or how serious it will be.

In notes to clients I usually say something to the effect that there is no way to know whether this will turn into something serious or be one we soon forget about. If it does become serious, we already know how it will end. It will just stop going down and then start to go back up, eventually making a new high. The only variable is that we don't know how long it will take.

I've included versions of that here on the blog too. It would be great to completely nail every downturn, but "don't let the pursuit of perfection be the enemy of pretty good" or words to that effect. If you care about going down less when the markets are going down and you are going down less, that's pretty good.

data.description:
Global equity markets shifted from orderly correction to broad liquidation dynamics overnight as Thursday’s steep Wall Street selloff spilt forcefully across Asia and Europe. The S&P 500 tumbled 2.0% to close near 7,176—logging its sixth consecutive decline and longest losing streak since 2024—while the Nasdaq and Dow Jones Industrial Average both shed over 2.0%, dragging the Dow below 50,000 for the first time since June. Crucially, the selloff occurred despite an ostensibly successful Nasdaq debut from Anthropic (ticker: ANT), which opened near $111.50 and closed at $97.17 (+17% above its $83 IPO price). When neither a blockbuster Nvidia beat nor the largest IPO in history can lift the tape, market psychology has fundamentally flipped from dip-buying to structural de-risking.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 cratered ~4.5%, South Korea’s Kospi lost ~5.0%, and Taiwan and Hong Kong faced aggressive liquidation as investors refused to extrapolate private-market AI appetite into public semiconductor upside amid US export-control scrutiny and capex return doubts. US equity futures remained heavy into the European open—with Nasdaq 100 contracts off 0.7% and DAX futures pointing toward 25,175—as deeply negative dealer gamma (~$100bn per 1% move) mechanically amplifies downside momentum below the 7,400–7,500 flip zone.

Cross-asset flows confirmed an acute defensive rotation. A resurgent safe-haven US Dollar bid dominated G10 FX, while Treasury yields eased marginally on risk-off demand yet remained constrained by hawkish Federal Reserve expectations ahead of next Wednesday’s October PCE print (seen rising toward 3.8% y/y). Despite the equity rout, spot Gold plunged toward $3,550/oz—tracking for one of its worst weeks in months—as elevated real yields, Dollar strength, and forced margin liquidations overwhelmed traditional haven demand. Copper retreated on global growth anxiety, while Brent crude held firm near $92.50/bbl after fresh tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz.

In the UK, domestic releases delivered a surprisingly constructive backdrop ahead of next week's Bank of England Treasury Select Committee testimony. October retail sales volumes excluding fuel surged 2.5% y/y (vs. 1.8% consensus), aided by government emergency-preparedness campaigns, though a 4.8% y/y retail deflator highlights persistent price friction that complicates any dovish reading of this week's softer CPI print. Concurrently, October Public Sector Net Borrowing printed £1bn better than consensus at £17.0bn, leaving cumulative cash requirements tracking roughly £9bn below prior OBR profiles and offering modest supply relief for gilts.

Macro to Micro: Financial markets have entered a mechanical liquidation regime where positive micro catalysts—from Nvidia earnings to Anthropic’s historic IPO—are being used as liquidity events to exit crowded exposures. Trapped deeply in negative gamma below 7,200–7,300, the S&P 500 remains vulnerable to dealer-driven selling pressure into the weekend against a backdrop of hawkish Fed pricing and real-yield strain. For traders, immediate tactical focus centers on S&P 500 put support at 7,000–7,200, ANT aftermarket stability, Dollar breakout momentum, Brent crude price action around Hormuz headlines, and next week's US PCE inflation test.

data.title: Gold Bounces Off September 2025 Low Amid Retreating USD; Fed Hike Bets To Cap Recovery
data.description:
Gold (XAU/USD) pares heavy intraday losses to its lowest level since September 2025, trading above $3,550 in the early European session on Friday, albeit retaining its bearish bias for the third straight day. A modest US Dollar (USD) pullback is seen as a key factor supporting the commodity. Meanwhile, traders are overwhelmingly pricing in a Federal Reserve (Fed) interest rate hike at its December policy meeting, which, along with fears of renewed US-Iran tensions, could limit USD losses and cap the non-yielding bullion.

Minutes from the October FOMC meeting, released on Wednesday, signaled a hawkish stance as nearly all officials expected further rate hikes to bring inflation back toward 2%. According to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool, a 25-basis-point (bps) rate increase at the next FOMC meeting in December is virtually a done deal. Moreover, financial markets are bracing for an extended stretch of restrictive US monetary policy well into next year. In fact, traders are pricing in a greater chance of additional hikes in January and April 2027. This has been a key factor behind the relentless selling of non-yielding gold witnessed over the past two weeks or so.

Dollar strength shifts from equity beta to Fed hawkishness

According to TD Securities, “upward US inflation momentum” has driven a regime change in FX, with markets now trading the USD “away from a relative equity regime to a hawkish Fed regime.” The bank notes that “the USD was trading in a relative equity regime for most of 2026 (Fig 2),” but it now trades under a framework “where the USD is supported by the US Treasury curve bear flattening dynamic (Fig 3) and market expectations of the Fed out-hawking other central banks (Fig 4).” In this setting, TD Securities argues that “the USD will likely remain resilient until Fed hawkishness peaks,” adding that “short-term relief for the bullish USD momentum could emerge with the Dec Fed SEP.” They see that peak in hawkishness as a key inflection point, cautioning that “the USD will likely remain resilient until Fed hawkishness peaks, which could play out under two scenarios,” to be further defined as the policy outlook becomes clearer.

On the geopolitical front, The New York Times reported that US President Donald Trump was considering another round of extensive military strikes on Iran. This comes on top of the US-Iran standoff over Tehran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz, helping the safe-haven USD trade within striking distance of its highest level since April 2025. However, extremely oversold conditions on short-term charts hold back traders from placing fresh bearish bets on gold amid a modest USD slide. Nevertheless, the XAU/USD pair seems poised to register losses for the second straight week and seems vulnerable to further losses.

XAU/USD daily chart

Technical Analysis

The XAU/USD pair extends a bearish phase following the recent breakdown below a horizontal support near the $3,900 mark. Moreover, the precious metal holds well below the technically significant 200-day Simple Moving Average (SMA) at $4,408.12, validating the negative outlook. Meanwhile, the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) indicator remains in negative territory with a widening downside profile. However, the Relative Strength Index (RSI) hovers near 24, signaling oversold conditions, which could slow, but not yet reverse, the prevailing downside pressure.

Hence, it will be prudent to wait for some near-term consolidation or a modest bounce before traders start positioning for an extension of the recent well-established downtrend. That said, any attempted recovery is more likely to be sold into and remain capped near the $3,900 support-turned-resistance. Moreover, a move beyond the 200-day SMA near $4,408.12 marks the level bulls would need to reclaim to ease the broader bearish bias.

data.title: Oracle's $23 Billion Cash-Flow Quarter Has An $11.4 Billion Timing Question
data.description:
Cloud demand is surging, but large customer prepayments, infrastructure spending, and new shares make future free cash flow per share the more demanding test.

Oracle (ORCL) reported $23.1 billion in operating cash flow for its fiscal first quarter ended August 31, 2026, up from $8.1 billion a year earlier. That sounds like compelling evidence that its AI infrastructure expansion is beginning to fund itself. The cash-flow statement, however, asks for a more careful reading: $11.36 billion came from an increase in deferred revenue tied to customer prepayments carrying a significant financing component. At the same time, Oracle spent $28.50 billion on capital expenditures.


Those prepayments are genuine cash, not a fictitious accounting entry. They can also indicate customers are willing to commit capital before receiving the contracted services. But cash received upfront is not the same as cash generated after delivering those services, and it is not automatically available as distributable free cash flow.

This distinction matters because Oracle is no longer being evaluated solely as a mature software company. Its fiscal first quarter cloud infrastructure revenue grew 121% to $7.4 billion, while total revenue increased 30% to $19.3 billion. Remaining performance obligations, or RPO, reached $664 billion, versus $455 billion one year earlier. The demand signals are substantial. The question is how they translate into durable cash generation after capacity is built and operated.

A cash-flow surge with two different drivers

The comparison is striking. In the quarter ended August 31, 2025, Oracle generated $8.14 billion in operating cash flow and spent $8.50 billion in capital expenditures, producing negative free cash flow of $0.36 billion. One year later, operating cash flow had reached $23.10 billion, but capital expenditures rose to $28.50 billion. Free cash flow therefore fell to negative $5.40 billion under Oracle's own definition: operating cash flow minus capital expenditures.

Figure 1. Fiscal first-quarter operating cash flow, capital expenditures and free cash flow (operating cash flow less capital expenditures), US$ billions. Source: Oracle Form 10-Q for the quarter ended August 31, 2026. Values rounded for display.

In other words, the company generated far more operating cash but spent even more building the infrastructure required to meet demand. That is not necessarily evidence of a bad investment. It is evidence that reported operating cash growth, by itself, cannot answer whether the buildout is becoming self-financing.

The financing component makes the comparison more nuanced. Oracle disclosed $11.363 billion of deferred-revenue growth from customer prepayments carrying a significant financing component in the current quarter, with no comparable amount in the year-earlier cash-flow statement. That represents about 49% of the $23.103 billion in operating cash flow reported this quarter. More strikingly, it equals approximately 76% of the $14.963 billion year-over-year increase in operating cash flow ($23.103 billion less $8.140 billion). Both percentages are arithmetic comparisons, not claims that the prepayments caused 49% of total cash generation or 76% of the change. Removing that single cash-flow line leaves $11.740 billion, but this is not a normalized operating cash-flow measure. Other working-capital movements matter, and the calculation says nothing about the profitability or eventual cash costs of delivering the prepaid contracts.

A $664 billion backlog has a long delivery schedule

Oracle estimates that only approximately 13% of its $664 billion RPO will be recognized as revenue in the next twelve months. It expects 37% in months 13 through 36, 34% in months 37 through 60, and the remaining 16% thereafter. These are management estimates of revenue recognition, not a timetable of profit realization or free-cash-flow collection.

Figure 2. Expected timing of revenue recognition from RPO as of August 31, 2026. Percentages are Oracle's estimates; the final 16% is the arithmetic remainder. Source: Form 10-Q.

This is both the opportunity and the risk. Multi-year commitments can increase demand visibility, making large capacity investments easier to justify. Yet the services still have to be delivered, the associated costs have to be incurred, and the expected margins must ultimately appear in reported results. Backlog should not be treated as cash already earned, or simply divided by a current-year revenue figure to infer a valuation multiple.

The commitments behind the capacity

There is another reason to separate contracted demand from realized cash economics. Oracle disclosed $288 billion in additional lease commitments, substantially all tied to data centers, that had not yet commenced and therefore were not reflected as liabilities on its August 31 balance sheet. These leases are generally expected to begin between the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2029, with terms of 15 to 19 years.

That $288 billion figure is not a bill due next quarter, nor is it directly comparable with RPO. Lease payments extend across many years, and the amounts represent different contractual relationships and timing conventions. It would be misleading to subtract $288 billion from the $664 billion backlog and present the result as an economic value. The relevant question is whether the cash earned from the underlying services over time will sufficiently cover data-center operating costs, lease commitments, and capital required to maintain the business.

Financing is already part of the picture. Oracle raised $19.9 billion in net proceeds by issuing approximately 141 million common shares through its at-the-market program during the quarter. Its reported common shares outstanding rose from 2.880 billion on May 31, 2026 to 3.024 billion on August 31, 2026, an increase of about 5%. Management also stated that it expected existing liquidity, operating cash generation, and available financing arrangements to cover obligations over at least the following twelve months. The capital raise supports liquidity and investment capacity, but it is not free cash generated by operating activities.

Oracle's cloud growth strengthens the demand case, but it does not by itself answer the per-share investment question. Investors therefore need to track whether contracted revenue eventually produces durable cash after the cost of building, operating and maintaining the required capacity, and how much of that cash accrues to each share as the share count changes. The larger share base is not, by itself, proof that the investment will destroy per-share value: financing could fund productive assets whose future economics more than compensate. A judgment about ORCL's valuation would also require a dated share price and explicit assumptions about future cash generation.

What would prove the thesis, or weaken it?

The constructive case is straightforward: AI-related cloud demand is growing rapidly; customers are committing to services years in advance; upfront payments reduce some near-term funding pressure; and large investments could eventually support attractive recurring economics. That argument deserves serious consideration.

The more skeptical case is also grounded in the filings: capital expenditures are running ahead of operating cash flow, customer financing materially affects the current cash-flow comparison, and very long-term infrastructure commitments introduce execution and utilization risks. Neither case can be settled using one quarter of data.

Over the next several reporting periods, I would follow four tests. First, how quickly does RPO become recognized cloud revenue? Second, do operating margins and cash collections improve after the associated capacity is delivered? Third, does free cash flow recover as capital spending moderates or utilization rises? Fourth, does free cash flow after investment improve on a per-share basis, taking account of any further share issuance, stock compensation and financing needs?

The most useful conclusion is not that Oracle's backlog is overstated or that its cash-flow improvement is illusory. It is that strong demand visibility and demonstrated cash profitability are different stages of the same investment thesis. Oracle has made the demand visible. The next test is how much lasting cash the contracts produce after the infrastructure is built, and how much of it ultimately belongs to each common share.

data.title: Japanese Yen Edges Higher As CPI Data Reinforces December BoJ Rate Hike Expectations
data.description:
The USD/JPY pair loses traction to around 159.20 during the early European trading hours on Friday. The Japanese Yen (JPY) edges higher against the US Dollar (USD) as Japan’s National Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation data boost expectations for Bank of Japan (BoJ) policy tightening.

Data released by the Japan Statistics Bureau on Friday showed that National Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation climbed to 2.3% YoY in October from 2.1% in September. Meanwhile, the core CPI, which strips out prices of food, rose 2.2% YoY in October, compared to 2.1% in the previous reading, below the market consensus of 2.3%. This figure exceeded the central bank's 2% target for the second straight month.

The index that strips ‌away the effects of both volatile fresh food and fuel, which is closely watched by the BoJ as a better gauge of demand-driven price pressures, increased 2.2% YoY in October, versus 2.4% prior.

Japan’s October inflation report is likely to push the BoJ toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 72% likelihood of a 25 basis points (bps) hike from the Japanese central bank.

On Thursday, BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said that underlying inflation roughly aligns with the price target. He added that the central bank plans to continue raising interest rates as monetary conditions remain accommodative.

USD/JPY tests 160 as BoJ signals December hike but flags yen risks

Strategists at Brown Brothers Harriman note that USD/JPY is “up and testing key resistance at 160.00,” with “higher US yields” keeping the pair “biased upward.” However, they caution that “intervention risk makes chasing gains beyond 160.00 a less attractive risk-reward trade.”

On the policy front, BBH highlights that BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda “reinforced expectations for a 25bps rate hike to 1.50% on December 18 (85% priced in).” Ueda “played down weak Q3 consumption spending, arguing the decline was in line with expectations and spending should recover.” He also “reiterated that financial conditions remain loose and warned that yen weakness could add to inflation pressures,” underscoring the central bank’s growing sensitivity to currency-driven price risks.

Ueda flags inflation overshoot risk as BoJ leans toward further tightening

Ueda’s 8/10 FXS Speechtracker score sits modestly above the historic 7.5/10 baseline, signalling a slightly more hawkish tilt as the Bank of Japan highlights both steady growth and “fragility” alongside a clear willingness to keep raising rates while financial conditions remain loose. Emphasis on underlying inflation aligning with the 2% target, the explicit risk of an inflation overshoot, and simulations showing accelerated ETF sales would not severely damage BoJ finances all reinforce a narrative that policy normalization can proceed without destabilizing markets.

The repeated focus on a weak Yen amplifying inflation via broader price pass-through, and the admission that FX swings now matter more for long-term inflation expectations, underscore a growing sensitivity to currency-driven upside inflation risks that supports a hawkish bias. Still, acknowledgement that rising crude prices and a weak Yen could squeeze real incomes and damp consumption, plus data showing only steady consumption as wages rise, gives Ueda cover to keep rate hikes gradual and data-dependent, with the pace and timing explicitly tied to the probability of the baseline outlook and associated risks.

Technical Analysis: USD/JPY maintains a constructive outlook above the 100-day SMA

In the daily chart, USD/JPY keeps a mild bullish bias as it holds above the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and the Bollinger middle band, suggesting underlying demand on shallow pullbacks. The Relative Strength Index (14) at 55 stays in positive but not overbought territory, hinting that upside momentum is constructive yet not stretched.

On the topside, immediate resistance is aligned with the upper Bollinger band near 160.30, where buyers could face profit-taking and volatility expansion. On the downside, initial support is seen at the 100-day SMA at 158.85, followed by the Bollinger mid-line at 158.65; a deeper retracement toward the lower Bollinger band around 157.00 would be needed to undermine the prevailing constructive tone.

data.title: Golden Squeeze: Record Gold Prices Meet Record Mining Costs
data.description:
Here’s a streak nobody in the gold business brags about. For 28 years in a row, the cost of mining an ounce of gold has gone up compared with the same quarter a year earlier.

“…the 28th consecutive year-on-year increase in AISC.”

World Gold Council and Metals Focus, August 24, 2026

AISC stands for all-in sustaining cost, the industry’s best measure of what it takes to keep a mine running and pull an ounce out of the ground. In the first quarter of 2026 it averaged $1,785 an ounce, up 16% from a year earlier. In the second quarter it hit a record $1,930, up 8% in three months and 22% in a year. That’s the fastest annual jump since 2013.

Some of that is the usual list. Diesel, freight, explosives, cyanide and replacement parts all got more expensive. The biggest driver, though, was the government’s cut. Royalty payments made up about 6% of the average miner’s costs in early 2021, and by early 2026 they’d doubled to about 12%. Ghana, for one, brought in a sliding-scale royalty in March 2026 that takes a bigger bite as the gold price climbs.

Now, to be fair, miners made money hand over fist this year. Gold averaged nearly $4,900 in the first quarter of 2026, and the World Gold Council put the average miner’s margin at a record $3,076 an ounce. At those prices, the average mine was a cash machine.

The catch is that costs only move in one direction, and the gold price doesn’t. Gold futures closed at $5,318 on January 29 and finished at $4,075 on November 6, down about 23%.

The Numbers

At $4,075 gold and $1,930 in costs, the average miner clears about $2,145 an ounce. That’s still a healthy business, but it’s about 30% less than the record margin from early this year, and that’s for the average mine. A high-cost producer, or one in a country that just raised its royalty, feels the drop first and feels it harder.

That’s how you can be right about gold and still lose money on a gold miner. The metal can hold most of its gains while a company with rising costs and a bigger tax bill watches its profit shrink.

So when I look at a miner, the first question isn’t how much gold it has. It’s what it costs to get that gold out, and how much the government takes along the way.

Next time, I’ll argue with my own thesis, because there’s way more gold out there than the doom crowd admits.

Sources: World Gold Council and Metals Focus, “Record gold prices outpace rising mining costs in Q1’26,” Gold Focus, August 24, 2026; World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends Q3 2026; Miningmx, November 3, 2026; Yahoo Finance, COMEX gold futures (GC=F). The margin at $4,075 gold is our own estimate: the November 6 futures close minus the Q2 2026 average AISC.

Markets are now pricing in nearly a 97.3% chance of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December, while there's a 2.7% odds of a larger 50-basis-point increase, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Higher rates are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest.

Metals slide and carry trades unwind as Dollar holds firm

Analysts at OCBC note that "concerns over AI spending, a hawkish shift in Fed expectations and hopes of Middle East de-escalation have triggered sharp moves across markets," with "industrial metals, particularly copper, [having] led the sell-off, while gold has also weakened." data.title: Disaster Survival Stocks: Companies That Could Benefit When Americans Prepare For The Worst
data.description:
The recent wave of technology outages, airline groundings, and disruptions to critical services has given Americans something new to think about: How prepared are we if the systems we depend on every day suddenly stop working?

On November 13, 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) experienced a telecommunications network failure that resulted in a nationwide ground stop. The disruption lasted approximately four hours and 45 minutes, with more than 12,000 flight cancellations reported that day. The problem affected 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. Although the FAA said that all aircraft landed safely, the incident demonstrated how a technical failure in one critical system can disrupt transportation across the country. 

There have also been other unsettling developments. United Airlines experienced a separate technology outage that disrupted flights at several major airports, including San Francisco International Airport. Meanwhile, the National Security Agency (NSA) experienced an outage of its internal classified information network on November 17. The NSA attributed the disruption to scheduled maintenance, and officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Nevertheless, the incident raised questions about the reliability of even highly sophisticated government computer systems. 

These events have fueled concerns about how vulnerable modern society has become to technology failures, cyberattacks, power outages, natural disasters, and interruptions in essential services. People increasingly recognize that electricity, communications, transportation, banking, and food distribution systems are interconnected. A problem in one area can quickly affect many others.

For investors, this raises an interesting question: Are there publicly traded companies that could benefit financially if more Americans begin preparing for emergencies?

There is an investment theme that could be called disaster survival stocks. These are companies that manufacture or sell products people may want to have available when normal services are interrupted. They include generators, emergency supplies, canned food, bottled water, home improvement products, ammunition, and other necessities.

The recent events have also brought renewed attention to a group of people known as preppers.

The Prepper Movement Goes Mainstream

Preppers are people who take steps to prepare for emergencies, ranging from relatively ordinary situations such as hurricanes, earthquakes, and extended power outages to more extreme possibilities such as widespread infrastructure failures, economic disruptions, and societal breakdowns.

Traditional preppers often maintain supplies of food and water, backup electricity, first-aid equipment, emergency communications devices, and other necessities. Some have installed solar panels, battery storage systems, and generators. Others maintain gardens, preserve their own food, store fuel, and develop plans for living without conventional utilities.

What is particularly interesting is that emergency preparedness is no longer limited to people who consider themselves survivalists.

A November 19, 2026, Washington Post report described Americans buying emergency supplies following the recent outages. Purchases included bottled water, canned food, battery-powered radios, portable generators, solar power stations, and propane supplies. One consumer reportedly spent approximately $3,500 expanding his emergency inventory. The article also reported unusually strong interest in generators at Costco, with 21 of the 26 most expensive generators listed on its website sold out as of the preceding Sunday. 

An additional report from Axios described a substantial increase in emergency-preparedness shopping, with one survival-gear retailer reporting a 450% increase in sales between October 27 and November 16 compared with preceding weeks. 

Whether these developments represent a temporary reaction to the headlines or the beginning of a longer-term trend remains to be seen. However, they could create opportunities for companies that supply the products associated with emergency preparedness.

Here are six publicly traded companies that investors and traders may want to investigate.

1. Olin Corporation (NYSE: OLN)

A Chemicals and Ammunition Play

Emergency supplies exposure

NYSE: OLN

Olin is an interesting, somewhat unconventional disaster-preparedness investment because it operates two businesses that could be relevant during periods of heightened emergency preparedness. Its Winchester division manufactures ammunition, including products for recreational shooting, hunting, law enforcement, and military applications. Its other operations produce chemicals, including chlorine, caustic soda, and epoxy products.

Ammunition is an established component of the prepper market, particularly among individuals interested in hunting, personal protection, and self-sufficiency. Increased consumer interest in emergency preparedness could potentially support ammunition demand, although Winchester’s business is much broader than the prepper market.

Olin reported third-quarter 2026 sales of approximately $1.75 billion and net income of $14.4 million, compared with $42.8 million in the prior-year quarter. Adjusted EBITDA was $191.4 million, down from $222.4 million. The company is also pursuing a merger with Huntsman, which it expects to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. 

Investment consideration: Winchester provides an interesting angle on the preparedness theme, but investors should remember that Olin is primarily a cyclical chemical company. Its earnings are sensitive to industrial demand, energy costs, chemical prices, and operating conditions. Its substantial debt and proposed merger also deserve attention.

2. The Home Depot (NYSE: HD)

The Emergency Repair and Equipment Play

NYSE: HD

Home Depot is one of the more obvious companies that could benefit when homeowners decide they need to become more self-sufficient. The company sells generators, power tools, flashlights, batteries, building materials, plumbing supplies, electrical equipment, and other products that become particularly important when homes experience damage or utility interruptions.

After a hurricane, wildfire, earthquake, or extended power outage, homeowners frequently need equipment and materials to restore their properties. Portable generators, extension cords, chainsaws, tarps, water pumps, and electrical supplies can all experience increased demand.

Home Depot also benefits from longer-term trends that have little to do with disasters, including aging housing stock, remodeling, maintenance, and professional contractor spending.

The company reported fiscal third-quarter 2026 sales of $43.4 billion, up 4.9% from the prior-year quarter. Comparable-store sales increased 2.2%, while earnings were $3.72 per diluted share. Management projected approximately 4.5% full-year sales growth for fiscal 2026. 

Investment consideration: Home Depot offers exposure to disaster-related repairs and preparedness without relying exclusively on emergency purchases. However, higher interest rates, weak housing turnover, and reduced consumer spending on remodeling could affect growth.

3. Generac Holdings (NYSE: GNRC)

The Backup Electricity Play

One of the most direct beneficiaries

NYSE: GNRC

Generac may be one of the most direct ways to invest in the disaster-preparedness trend. The company manufactures standby generators, portable generators, battery storage systems, and other energy technology products.

For homeowners, a standby generator can automatically provide electricity when the utility grid goes down. This can be particularly important for people who depend on electricity for medical equipment, refrigeration, heating, air conditioning, security systems, and communications.

The company also sells commercial and industrial backup power systems. Hospitals, data centers, telecommunications facilities, businesses, and other critical operations require dependable backup electricity.

An especially interesting development is the growing demand for backup power from data centers. Generac announced a long-term supply agreement with Amazon that includes an expected $2.4 billion in initial generator deliveries during 2027 and 2028.

Generac’s third-quarter 2026 results were impressive. Net sales increased 16% to a record $1.29 billion, while net income rose to $109 million from $66 million in the prior-year quarter. Residential sales increased approximately 9%, supported by stronger demand for home standby and portable generators. The company maintained its full-year sales growth guidance in the mid-to-high teens percentage range. Its data-center product backlog reached approximately $4.5 billion. 

Investment consideration: Generac is particularly attractive as a way to participate in the longer-term need for backup electricity, including data-center demand. However, the stock can be sensitive to weather patterns, residential construction, interest rates, and the timing of generator purchases. Competition and execution risks associated with its expanding industrial business should also be considered.

4. The Campbell’s Company (Nasdaq: CPB)

The Shelf-Stable Food Play

Nasdaq: CPB

Food is one of the most basic components of emergency preparedness. When people worry about disruptions to grocery stores, transportation, or electricity, they often begin stocking their pantries with products that have long shelf lives.

Campbell’s is well positioned in this category through its soup, canned food, sauces, snacks, and other packaged food products. Its well-known brands include Campbell’s, Prego, Pace, Swanson, and Goldfish.

Canned soup and other shelf-stable foods are particularly useful during emergencies because they can be stored for extended periods and many varieties can be consumed with little preparation.

Unlike companies that sell generators or emergency equipment, Campbell’s has a business that is not dependent on consumers making large discretionary purchases. Food is something people need regardless of economic conditions.

However, investors should be aware that Campbell’s has recently encountered financial difficulties. For fiscal 2026, annual sales declined 5% to $9.7 billion, while adjusted earnings per share declined 27% to $2.17. The company announced a dividend reset as part of a strategy to accelerate debt reduction. It is also targeting $500 million in cost savings by fiscal 2030. 

Investment consideration: Campbell’s offers defensive consumer staples exposure, but investors should not assume that increased emergency food purchases will automatically translate into substantial earnings growth. Competition, consumer preferences, food input costs, and the company’s debt reduction efforts are important considerations.

5. Walmart (Nasdaq: WMT)

The Essential Goods Distribution Play

Nasdaq: WMT

Walmart could be one of the biggest beneficiaries of increased consumer interest in emergency preparedness simply because of its enormous retail distribution network.

The company sells virtually everything consumers might need during an emergency, including bottled water, canned food, batteries, flashlights, first-aid supplies, over-the-counter medications, blankets, coolers, portable power equipment, and household necessities.

Its combination of physical stores, distribution centers, and e-commerce operations gives it an advantage in making essential products available to consumers. Walmart’s grocery business is particularly important because food represents a large portion of household emergency supplies.

There is also an important distinction between Walmart and some of the other companies discussed here. Walmart does not need a major disaster to generate sales. It sells everyday necessities that consumers purchase regularly, regardless of whether they are preparing for an emergency.

Walmart reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $188.8 billion on November 19, 2026, an increase of 5.2%. E-commerce sales increased 17% globally, and the company raised its full-year outlook. Operating income increased 16%. 

Investment consideration: Walmart offers a relatively diversified way to participate in the emergency-preparedness theme. Its scale, pricing power, and everyday grocery business provide some defensive characteristics. However, its valuation, labor costs, competitive pressures, and retail profit margins should be examined before purchasing shares.

6. Costco Wholesale (Nasdaq: COST)

The Bulk Purchasing and Stockpiling Play

Recent demand evidence

Nasdaq: COST

Costco might be one of the most interesting companies in this group because its warehouse business is naturally suited to consumers who want to purchase large quantities of essential goods.

Its merchandise includes bulk bottled water, canned food, paper products, batteries, first-aid supplies, household necessities, and emergency equipment. Costco also sells generators and other power-related products.

The membership warehouse model encourages consumers to buy larger quantities than they might purchase at a conventional grocery store. This is particularly attractive to households that want to maintain an emergency supply of food and other essentials.

There is already evidence that recent events have generated increased interest in Costco’s emergency-preparedness merchandise.

According to a November 2026 report citing Mizuho Securities, 21 of the 26 most expensive generators listed on Costco’s website were sold out as of November 15. Analysts also attributed some of the company’s stronger October comparable-store sales to emergency-preparedness purchases. 

Costco reported fiscal 2026 annual sales of approximately $297.2 billion, up 10.1% from the previous year. Fourth-quarter net income increased to approximately $3.0 billion from $2.61 billion. Its October 2026 sales increased 12.6% to $24.5 billion. 

Investment consideration: Costco has an attractive business model, recurring membership income, and a loyal customer base. It could benefit from increased stockpiling, but emergency purchases are only a small part of its overall business. Its valuation is also an important consideration. Investors should avoid assuming that a temporary surge in preparedness shopping justifies paying an excessive earnings multiple.

Other stocks worth investigating

The six companies above are not the only publicly traded businesses that could benefit from increased emergency preparedness.

These companies provide additional exposure to different aspects of emergency preparedness, from portable power and food production to water infrastructure and home repairs.

What Are the Biggest Investment Risks?

Although disaster preparedness is an interesting investment theme, investors should distinguish between a temporary increase in consumer purchases and a sustained change in spending behavior.

A major outage or natural disaster can produce a sudden increase in demand for generators, bottled water, canned food, batteries, and other supplies. However, consumers may already have purchased these products, reducing the need for repeat purchases.

For example, a household that buys a generator may not need another one for 10 or 15 years. Similarly, people who stock their pantries with canned goods may not need to replenish their supplies immediately.

There is also the risk that investors will overreact to headlines. A stock can rise substantially on expectations of higher demand even if the actual increase in company earnings is relatively small.

Valuation is especially important. Costco, for example, has a strong business, but its shares have historically commanded a premium valuation. Campbell’s has a more defensive food business, but its recent financial results illustrate that even companies selling essential products can experience declining earnings.

Finally, these companies are exposed to different economic forces. Olin is affected by industrial chemical demand, Generac by generator purchasing cycles and data-center investment, and Home Depot by the housing and remodeling markets.

Conclusion: Building a Disaster-Preparedness Investment Watchlist

The recent technology outages, airline disruptions, and NSA network incident have highlighted an important vulnerability of modern society: We depend on interconnected systems that can sometimes fail unexpectedly.

Whether these incidents prove to be isolated technical problems or part of a broader trend, they have reminded consumers of the importance of having backup plans.

From an investment perspective, I would put Generac near the top of the list because it provides direct exposure to backup electricity, a market that has opportunities beyond residential emergency preparedness, particularly with data centers. Home Depot is another interesting candidate because it sells the equipment and materials needed to prepare for and recover from disasters.

Walmart and Costco provide exposure to consumers stocking up on necessities, while Campbell’s offers exposure to shelf-stable food. Olin is a more specialized investment, with its Winchester ammunition business providing an additional angle on the preparedness market.

I would be particularly interested in monitoring whether the recent increase in emergency-preparedness shopping translates into sustained sales growth over the next several quarters. If consumers begin making preparedness a regular part of household budgeting rather than simply reacting to alarming headlines, some of these companies could benefit from a meaningful long-term business trend.

The key for investors and traders is not to bet on a disaster occurring. It is to identify companies that sell products people increasingly value because they want to be prepared if one does.

data.title: Anthropic Makes Historic Debut, AMD Falls 8%
data.description:
Anthropic (ANT) shares surged 34.3% initially after making their Nasdaq debut, pushing the AI company's market valuation above $2 trillion.

AMD (AMD) fell 8% after an investigation by Hunterbrook Media alleged that its firmware was being used by a blacklisted Chinese server maker and related businesses.

Gold dropped to a 14-month low as a stronger dollar and expectations of higher US interest rates weighed on bullion.

Oil prices recovered as reports of tanker disruptions and escalating tensions around the Strait of Hormuz raised concerns about Middle Eastern supply.

Anthropic stock jumps 34% in record IPO debut

Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT, opening at $111.50 a share after pricing its IPO at $83.

The company raised more than $81 billion through the sale of approximately 980 million shares, making it the largest IPO on record.

Shares climbed 34.3% after opening, taking the company's valuation above $2 trillion. This placed Anthropic behind Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Nvidia (NVDA), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Amazon (AMZN) in market capitalisation.

The stock pared gains and was trading 14% up at the time of writing.

The offering was led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, with JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Barclays also serving as underwriters.

The debut is significant for the wider AI sector because Anthropic is the first major AI laboratory to go public.

Its shares could become a benchmark for investor appetite towards AI companies as markets assess whether substantial spending on models and computing infrastructure can generate sustainable returns.

Co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell.

Dario Amodei reiterated the company's commitment to AI safety, saying it would not bend to business or political pressure.

Anthropic could also benefit from Nasdaq's revised index inclusion rules, which allow eligible large-cap companies to qualify for fast-track inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 after 15 trading days.

Intropic estimates that index-tracking funds could purchase around 333 million shares across four dates during the first month.

AMD stock falls 8% on China exposure allegations

AMD shares declined 8% after Hunterbrook Media alleged that the company's firmware was being used by IEIT Systems, a Chinese server maker placed on the US government's Entity List in March 2025.

The investigation identified at least six newer versions of AMD firmware in IEIT products after the blacklisting.

It also alleged that three companies in China, Singapore and California offered servers containing closely matching firmware.

Hunterbrook said corporate filings indicated links between IEIT and some of these businesses.

The report also raised questions about AMD licensing income from two Chinese chip ventures previously blacklisted by US authorities.

The allegations have drawn attention to AMD's exposure to export restrictions at a time when investors have viewed it as an alternative to Nvidia.

Hunterbrook disclosed that its affiliated investment firm was short AMD shares and held long positions in comparable securities.

Gold hits 14-month low as rate expectations rise

Spot gold fell 1.45% to $3,668.27 an ounce, after touching $3,667.19, its lowest level since September 2025. US gold futures settled 1.85% lower at $3,672.50.

A stronger US dollar and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy weighed on bullion.

The dollar index reached its highest level since April 2025, making dollar-priced gold more expensive for overseas buyers.

Markets were pricing in a 94% chance of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December and a 6% probability of a 50-basis-point move.

Higher interest rates reduce the appeal of non-yielding assets such as gold.

Silver, platinum and palladium also declined.

Oil rises as Strait of Hormuz risks return

Brent crude gained 0.29% to $92.22 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate rose 0.58% to $83.74.

Reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz supported prices after the previous session's decline, which was driven by rising US inventories and expectations of a supply surplus.

Iran's navy said two oil tankers hit naval mines and exploded in the strait.

Meanwhile, Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh added to regional tensions.

However, concerns about ample supply continued to limit gains.

Saudi crude exports rose nearly 21% in September to 5.38 million barrels per day, while a larger-than-expected increase in US inventories reinforced concerns about a potential surplus.

After another day of losses, the US S&P 500 index is now 8.5% off its highs of the year. The extent of this correction is not far from that seen in March this year (9.5%) and way off the 'Liberation Day' rout of 21% seen in March/April 2025. The cause of the current correction has been the threat of a faster Federal Reserve tightening cycle, put on the table by the Fed's Christopher Waller last week. We discussed high US real interest rates here yesterday. And the volatility in tech stocks may also be owing to this week's Anthropic IPO, where investors have probably been shuffling portfolios to participate in a $100bn IPO. The fact that the Fed wants to tighten faster because of a demand shock should not necessarily be bad news for equities and, barring some major earning misses, the case for another 10% correction in equities is a weak one.

Yet there seems no reason for the Fed to drop its hawkish rhetoric anytime soon. Next Wednesday sees the release of the Fed's preferred inflation measure – the core PCE index. The October data is expected to show the year-on-year rate rising to 3.2% with upside risks, and confirm that the Fed will need to take action.

For FX, that means a continued strong dollar and continued pressure on popular carry trades. The Latam complex has had a terrible week, with the most popular carry position, the Colombian peso, off heavily. Brazil yesterday stepped in with FX intervention, but $1bn in sales was quickly overwhelmed. Elsewhere, the big drop in metals has left the South African rand vulnerable, and a dovish central bank has seen an unwind of crowded positions in Hungary's forint. We are also starting to see expectations build for rate cuts in Australia next year on the view that the Reserve Bank of Australia has overtightened. We highlighted this as one of the key risks in our 2027 FX Outlook. Pressure may also be building on long positions in the Turkish lira, where implied yields are starting to rise again.

A big carry trade unwind and emerging markets sell-off remain a positive for the dollar, and to a lesser degree, the yen. We expect the dollar to hold gains into next week and keep 104.60 as a near-term DXY target.

The US data calendar is light today, and the only Fed speakers are the hawkish Waller (10:15CET) and Lisa Cook, who surprisingly voted for a hike at the October FOMC meeting.

Chris Turner

EUR: Correction in risk assets doesn't help the euro

EUR/USD continues to consolidate below 1.10. Our FX options traders suggest the low volatility price action here is a function of a lot of FX options barriers in the 1.0850-1.0950 area. Nonetheless, a correction in risk assets – and especially a correction in emerging market currencies – is typically dollar-positive, and we expect EUR/USD to face continuing downside risks. 1.0880 remains the potential for this move.

On the calendar is the release of eurozone negotiated wages for the third quarter. These are expected at 2.6% year-on-year, way off the 4-5% levels seen in 2024-2025 that would have worried the European Central Bank with the threat of second-round effects.

Elsewhere in Europe, the Hungarian forint is under heavy pressure. The National Bank of Hungary's dovish tilt at this week's meeting won't have helped, but long forint positions would always have been vulnerable to a global carry trade unwind. So far, positions in the long end of the Hungarian local currency bond market have been untouched – this is where investors are positioned for Hungary's euro story. Any sharp spike in these bond yields would caution a deeper correction to the Hungary story and even more pressure on the forint. Any EUR/HUF close above the 373.65 upside gap from April would warn of an extension to 380.

Chris Turner

GBP: New EU-UK agreements announced

At a press conference in Brussels today, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders are expected to announce three new agreements. The first is on SPS (Sanitary and Phytosanitary measures), which will reduce border checks on trade in food, animals and plants. The second is on a greater alignment between the separate EU and UK Emissions Trading Schemes (ETS), where greater recognition of each other's schemes can reduce carbon-related friction in trade – especially important for the steel and manufacturing sectors. The third looks at the thorny issue of mobility in the Youth Experience Scheme (YES), where up to 100,000 18-31 year-olds can obtain work visas for up to three years. Burnham will be marketing these deals as addressing the cost-of-living crisis and giving young Britons valuable opportunities overseas.

The deals, as always, will be subject to last-minute negotiation and serve as a reminder to the Burnham government that 'cherry-picking' the best parts of a relationship with the EU is no easy task. That may sway the Labour Party against any commitment to rejoin the EU in its next election manifesto – which could potentially emerge as early as next year.

Sterling typically responds well to the prospect of closer UK ties with Europe on the view that reversing a bad Brexit deal can generate a 1-2% larger UK economy in 5-10 years' time. Today's agreements are fully expected, however, and may not generate any independent sterling strength.

That said, we like sterling over the coming months on the view that Bank of England tightening expectations prove more resilient than those of the ECB. This corrective EUR/GBP rally may again stall in the 0.8400 area, and we are happy with a year-end forecast of 0.8300.

Chris Turner

Latam: $1bn Brazil intervention is not enough

USD/BRL briefly corrected yesterday when the Central Bank of Brazil announced it would conduct an auction to sell US$1 billion. Gains in the Brazilian real were only fleeting, with investors still wary that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has no interest in fiscal consolidation. Back in late 2024, BCB had to increase the size of its spot USD auction to $3-5bn to provide stability to the real. We cannot rule out USD/BRL extending to the 6.00/6.30 region again, but imagine investors would start to find those levels as attractive again for the real and its high real interest rates.

Elsewhere, USD/MXN is trading comfortably through 19.00. This outcome cannot have been unexpected for Banxico after it cut rates in November. 19.60 is now the risk, assuming the dollar stays strong.

The Brutal (& Stealthy) Tech Bear Market

Having traded a plethora of difficult market environments, including COVID, the Global Financial Crisis, the Tariff Tantrum, and the 2022 bear market, I can confidently say that the 2026 market is one of the most difficult trading environments I can remember – if not the most difficult. The choppiness, whiplash, and violent direction changes make navigation challenging. Additionally, the sheer number of crosscurrents is more than I can ever remember. Until recently, higher oil prices and inflation concerns from the Iran War have weighed down stocks. Although oil prices have cooled significantly in recent weeks, the focus has turned to the AI trade. Despite unprecedented CAPEX spending, AI stocks have plunged.

Currently, the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index ETF (QQQ - Free Report) is ~15% off its all-time highs, triggering a market correction. While QQQ has yet to trigger a technical bear market (defined as a 20% drawdown from highs), most AI stocks have been pummeled and are already in bear-market territory. Below are some examples of AI stocks and their % off highs:

Nvidia (NVDA - Free Report): -40%

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD - Free Report): -26%

SanDisk (SNDK - Free Report) -68%

Nebius Group (NBIS - Free Report): -68%

Arm Holdings (ARM - Free Report): -61%

The Tech Trade is Reaching a Tipping Point

As the old Wall Street saying goes, “Sometimes when you try to pick bottoms, all you end up with is stinky fingers.” Currently, the bears are firmly in control of the market. The Nasdaq is below the 200-day moving average, AI’s most important CEO is out of a job, and interest rates are expected to keep moving higher. For intermediate-term investors, it’s critical to first and foremost protect capital and wait for confirmation in the form of improved market breadth and price rotation on higher time frames. If you need to reduce portfolio size, do so. The market is not going anywhere. Until then, avoid picking up pennies in front of a steamroller.

Nevertheless, if there’s one thing that I have learned throughout my years of investing experience, it’s that even if you’re a spectator, the market is still worth following closely. That’s because crisis ultimately equates to opportunity. Throughout American history, the market always exits these tough environments leading to massive opportunities. Additionally, equity markets are the master manipulator - bottoms are never obvious and often occur when they are least expected.

Market Extremes Pile Up

On Thursday, several extremes occurred on Wall Street, including:

·       Tech Valuations Reach Pandemic Lows: The S&P 500 Info Tech Index’s price-to-earnings ratio has plunged to 15x.

Image Source: Bloomberg

·       Rare, Violent Reversal: According to my friends at BlueKurtic Market Insights (@Bluekurtic), when QQQ starts the day 1.5% and finishes red, the chances of a low actually increase. Image Source: Bluekurtic Market Insights

·       TICK Prints Multi-Month Lows: The TICK is a real-time market breadth indicator that measures short-term buying versus selling pressure on the New York Stock Exchange. On Thursday, TICK reached its most extreme selling level (-1448) in months. Often, a TICK washout of this nature is needed to flush out the last remaining bulls.

Some Market Hurdles are About to Pass

Market headwinds such as the Jensen Huang Nvidia exit, Anthropic IPO, and options expiration may provide much-needed relief for bulls. Huang was undoubtedly the most critical CEO for the tech trade. According to Elon Musk and others, he’s one of one. However, as investors come to terms with his exit, it’s worth noting that time is the ultimate healer.

Anthropic (ANT - Free Report), one of the most anticipated IPOs in history, debuted this week.Priced at $83, ANT shares soared to ~$110 intraday before encountering profit-taking and reversing course. The average Anthropic employee is now worth an astonishing $40 million. Billions of shares traded hands, marking one of the busiest IPOs in history. Despite the hysteria, investors sold shares of their current holdings to invest in Anthropic, putting downward pressure on the rest of the market.

Finally, options expiration was on Friday. Options expiration frequently triggers market turning points because dealers unwinding or rolling large option hedges—alongside expiring gamma pin levels and pinning magnets—forcing rapid rebalancing in underlying shares and index futures that can either release pent-up directional momentum or spark sharp mean reversion once the distortion clears.

Bottom Line

For now, the name of the game is capital preservation. That said, investors should stay positive and open-minded as markets can change on a dime.

data.title: Eliminate Sleepless Nights: Stop Worrying About Market Changes
data.description:
It is 3 a.m. and you are awake again, staring at the ceiling, doing arithmetic you cannot control. The market moved yesterday. It will move today. You own the metal, or you are thinking about buying it, and either way the question running circles in your head is the same one: did I do it right?

I have watched this market for five decades. Let me tell you the single most valuable thing I learned, and it is not a price target. It is this: the investor who sleeps well is not the one who predicts the market. It is the one who removed the need to predict it.

Here is how you do that.

Step One: Decide the End Objective First

Before you buy a single ounce of anything, answer one question in writing: what is this money for?

- Was it growth? You want the position to multiply, and you accept the swings that come with that.
- Asset preservation? You want what you have built to still be there, intact, when the storm passes.
- Maintaining purchasing power? You want your savings to buy in twenty years what they buy today.
- Posterity legacy? You want to hand something real to the generations that follow you.

At SilverScoreboard, we are primarily interested in building a legacy for the generations that follow them. That changes everything about how you behave — because a legacy holder is not racing anybody to an exit.

Most sleepless nights come from a position that does not know what it is for. Growth money held with legacy nerves. Legacy money checked with a trader's stopwatch. Decide the objective first, and half the worry dies right there, because now every market move has a context: does this change what the money is for? Almost never.

Investment vs. Hedge: The Intent Sets the Clock

This is where we must understand the difference between an investment and a hedge.

An investment is made to grow. You measure it against what you paid, and you watch the clock: is it working, how fast, compared to what?

A hedge is made to stand beside the rest of your savings — to hold value when other things fall, and especially to stand against inflation, which quietly eats away the nest egg year after year without ever making a headline.

The intent changes your mindset and the timeline on your expectations. A growth investment asks "how much, by when?" A hedge asks "is it still doing its job?" Those are different questions, and only one of them lets you sleep. If you hold physical precious metals as a hedge against inflation, a Tuesday price move is not a verdict on your decision. It is weather.

"Be Anxious for Nothing" — Is That Actually Possible?

Biblically, we are instructed not to worry. "Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and supplication with gratitude, make your requests known to God" (Philippians 4:6, MEV).

Is that possible with money at stake? I believe it is — not by willpower, but by structure. Worry lives in the gap between your responsibility and your control. Shrink that gap and the worry shrinks with it.

That is exactly what Dollar Cost Averaging does. It is a simple strategy that can eliminate multiple decisions and a lot of sleepless nights, because it replaces the question that tortures people — is now the right time? — with an answer that never changes: it is always the right time for the next planned purchase.

What Dollar Cost Averaging Actually Is

Let us define it plainly. Dollar Cost Averaging is the practice of investing a fixed dollar amount into the same asset on a fixed schedule — the same dollars, the same day, every month — regardless of price.

That last phrase carries the whole strategy. Not "when it feels right." Not "when the news quiets down." Regardless of price. When the price is high, your fixed dollars buy fewer ounces. When the price is low, the identical dollars buy more. You never make a market call; you make a standing appointment.

What It Buys You Over Time

The advantages compound the way the metal does:

- It removes the timing decision. Buying at highs on excitement and selling at lows on fear is the oldest mistake in investing. A standing purchase cannot panic and cannot chase.
- It turns falling prices into more metal. The dip that ruins a lump-sum buyer's year is quietly loading your shelf. Volatility stops being the enemy and becomes the discount.
- It averages your cost across every market climate instead of pinning your whole result to one emotional afternoon.
- It builds the habit that builds the legacy. Month after month, year after year, the stack grows on schedule whether the headlines are roar or whisper.
- It starves regret. There is no "I bought the top" story to tell, because every purchase was simply the plan arriving on time.

How the Strategy Works: The Same Dollars, the Same Day, Every Month

Dollar Cost Averaging means committing a fixed, dedicated percentage of your income to precious metals purchases on a regular basis over time — month after month, year after year. Not what feels right. Not what the news suggests. A number, chosen once, honored every month.

How do you calculate the number? Three steps:

1. Pick the percentage. Many families dedicate somewhere between five and ten percent of monthly income to their metal. The right number is the one you can keep through a bad month without touching the grocery money.
2. Convert it to dollars. Five percent of a $6,000 monthly income is $300. That is your purchase, every month, same day if possible. Automate it or calendar it so no monthly decision exists.
3. Buy the metal. The same dollar amount every time. When silver is high, your dollars buy fewer ounces. When silver is low, they buy more. That is the entire engine.

Here is a real twelve-month example — $300 a month through a swinging market (illustrative prices):

Month             Price/oz          Ounces bought     Total ounces
  1                 $72.00            4.167             4.167
  3                 $64.00            4.688             13.234
  5                 $61.50            4.878             23.284
  7                 $70.50            4.255             32.085
  9                 $59.00            5.085             41.894
  11                $67.00            4.478             51.172
  12                $71.00            4.225             55.397

Total spent: $3,600. Total metal: more than fifty-five ounces — nearly four pounds in a single year. Average cost: $64.99 an ounce — in a year where the average price was $65.29 and the anxious buyer's first purchase was $72.00.

Notice what the strategy did not require: no prediction, no timing, no decision after decision after decision. The buyer who lump-summed at the top out of fear of missing out paid $72. The disciplined buyer averaged $64.99 without once needing to be right about anything. Twelve decisions became zero decisions. That is what eliminates the sleepless nights — not willpower, arithmetic.

Run the same $300 for five years and you have roughly 277 ounces — nineteen pounds of metal — accumulated without a single midnight decision. Ten years, and the legacy is unmistakable: 554 ounces, thirty-eight pounds, an asset with five thousand years of history behind it, and something your grandchildren can hold in their hands. Precious metals have a 5,000-year history and have never been worth zero. No paper currency in history can make that claim.

The Same Strategy Works in Stocks and Bonds — With Different Sleep

Let the reader be clear-eyed about this: Dollar Cost Averaging is not a metals-only trick. The very same strategy can apply to investments in stocks and bonds, and it is the classic form there too — the same dollars into the same index fund or the same bond ladder, every month, on schedule. The arithmetic of averaging works identically.

But there is a difference, and I would not be honest if I hid it. If you choose stocks and bonds, you have to accept worry in your life.

A company can fail. A bond can default. A currency can be printed into oblivion. Paper wealth has counterparties — somebody's promise standing between you and your money — and promises, however respectable, can break. Dollar Cost Averaging into paper smooths your entry price; it cannot smooth away the question of whether the thing itself endures. That question is the worry, and it never quite goes to zero.

Metal is different. Precious metals have a 5,000-year history and have never been worth zero. No paper asset — no stock, no bond, no currency in history — can make that claim. So the same discipline buys you two different nights of sleep: in paper, a disciplined strategy and a residue of worry; in metal, a disciplined strategy and the quiet that comes from holding something that cannot go broke.

Growth money and hedge money can live in the same house. Just know which dollar is which, and let the hedge be the part you never lose sleep over.

Watching the Stack Without Watching the Clock

One honest note on tools, because a hedge you never measure is a hope, not a plan. When you own physical metal, the only question that matters at any moment is "what is the whole stack worth today?" — and that is a living number, moving with the market. I built the SilverScoreboard to answer exactly that question: the signals that move metals, side by side with a running total of what you hold, so a $2 afternoon move is information instead of alarm. Check it once a week, the way a farmer checks the barometer — then go back to sleep.

The Standard Caveats

Dollar Cost Averaging does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss in a declining market; it is a discipline, not a prediction. Precious metals prices are volatile and can fall as well as rise. The percentages here are illustrations, not recommendations, and nothing in this article is financial advice — it is financial literacy, which is a different and more durable asset.
