data.title: Anthropic's ANT Closes At $97.17, Up 17% On Its First Day Of Trading
data.description:
Anthropic’s Class A shares, ticker ANT, closed at $97.17 on their first day on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on 19 November 2026.

That is about 17% above the $83.00 IPO price set a day earlier, and about 13% below the $111.50 opening print.

The day began in Times Square, where co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the Nasdaq opening bell at 9:30am ET. The ceremony itself did not start trading in ANT. The first trade came later, at 16:50 GMT (11:50am ET), when the shares opened at $111.50, about 34% above the offering price.

Indications had been climbing through the morning, from about $99.60 to $105, then $110 and $111, before the stock opened slightly above that last level. The early burst did not last.

ANT peaked at $115.10 just before noon ET and slipped as low as $92.72.

By mid-afternoon the shares were changing hands around $95.60, still about 15% above the IPO price. The $97.17 close left the debut comfortably above the offering, but well short of the opening pop.

Even so, a 17% first-day gain on the largest IPO on record is a strong debut, the more so on a session in which the main US indexes finished more than 2% lower. The market took some of the opening froth off, but buyers who received stock at $83 still ended the day well in the money.

More than 846 million shares changed hands, ahead of the 522 million traded on SpaceX’s opening day in June, and enough to make ANT the most actively traded name on the Nasdaq. Volume had already passed 640 million by mid-session.

At the $111.50 open, Reuters put Anthropic’s market value at about $2 trillion, a level exceeded by only a handful of US-listed firms, and ahead of the $1.96 trillion it assigned to SpaceX at its June opening trade. That is a reported valuation at the open, not a closing figure.

The fade came as the wider market turned lower. US stocks ended more than 2% down. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 1,101.11 points, or 2.19%, to 49,097.06, the S&P 500 fell 2.02% to 7,175.83, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to 23,879.20.

AI shares were mixed as investors weighed worries about higher interest rates. The Nasdaq itself had been up as much as 2% after the open before those gains were given back.

The listing is the first by a frontier AI lab and sets a public-market benchmark for the group, with OpenAI still private. Ordinary investors now have a listed way to take a direct view on a stand-alone model developer, rather than only through the chipmakers and cloud groups that have dominated the trade.

Anthropic sold 980 million Class A shares at $83.00 on Wednesday, of which 956,351,354 were sold by the company and 23,648,646 by selling stockholders. The deal raised about $81.3 billion, making it the largest initial public offering on record, above SpaceX’s initial $75 billion.

The size and price had already been lifted once before the open. Last week the company had marketed 825 million shares at $70 to $78; on Wednesday it sold more stock, and at a higher price, than that range implied. SpaceX later reached $85.7 billion after its overallotment was exercised.

Anthropic’s underwriters have the option to buy up to a further 147 million Class A shares, which would bring in another $12.2 billion and take the IPO total to $93.5 billion if exercised. They have until 20 November to take up that option. The offering itself is expected to close on 20 November, subject to customary conditions.

The banks on the deal are due about $550 million in underwriting fees, according to the company’s filing, more than the roughly $500 million paid on the SpaceX IPO.

The company priced the offering above its marketed range and increased the number of shares being sold, initially valuing the Claude developer at $1.5 trillion. Investors who received an allocation pay the $83 offering price. Anyone buying once the shares are listed pays the market price, which closed at $97.17.

Demand was unusually lopsided. Retail interest in the IPO was the largest in history. Anthropic prioritized institutional investors it already knew, and roughly half of the firms that placed orders were left empty-handed, a higher share than usual.

Retail allocation came in at around 15%, below the roughly 20% the company had targeted, though still above the 5% to 10% typical in most IPOs.

Analysts who opened coverage stayed above the close. Melius started at Buy with a $155 price target; Ben Reitzes, the firm’s head of technology research, said that assigned value could even be “conservative”. Needham’s Scott Berg has a Buy rating and a $150 target. The average target across five Buy ratings was about $116.

Wolfe Research, in a Thursday note, said cybersecurity could match Anthropic’s coding opportunity and reach $500 billion annually.

The company has given a sense of the scale behind that interest. In its prospectus, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion of revenue in the nine months to 30 September, up about 1,200% from the same period a year earlier, and that its run-rate revenue was about $81 billion by the end of October.

What comes next is tightly timetabled. Index funds will not add the stock immediately. The Morningstar US Total Market Index will include it after five trading days, the Nasdaq-100 after 18 December, and the S&P 500 will not add it for at least a year.

About 15.5 billion insider shares are subject to lock-up agreements that run until after Anthropic reports results in the third quarter of next year. No date has been set for the first earnings report.

The official terms of the offering are in our report on Anthropic’s official IPO pricing. The first print is covered in our report on how ANT opened.

The wider timetable is on our Anthropic IPO date, valuation and ticker hub. For access and why the open-market price is not $83, see how to buy Anthropic stock.

data.title: Cheaper Gasoline Is Coming
data.description:
James Thorne of Wellington Altus tweeted an important graph and commentary worth reviewing. The US 3-2-1 crack spread, which approximates what a refiner earns by turning three barrels of crude into two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillates, has fallen 36% in six weeks, from $65.56 on October 9 to $41.90 on November 17. As he puts it, “the glut has moved downstream.”

The evidence supports his view. Fat profit margins enticed refiners to run at maximum capacity and boost their profits as much as possible. As one would think, with falling crack spreads, gasoline and diesel prices are falling faster than crude as supply rises rapidly. AAA shows the national gasoline price average near $3.75, down roughly 13% in a month, and the gasoline ETF UGA has dropped about 21% month to date. Gasoline futures have fallen about 45% over the last two months from $3.63 on September 24 to its current level of $2.50. Because retail pump prices lag wholesale/futures by weeks, the AAA pump price should fall further.

Over the last four decades, the 3-2-1 spread averages roughly $12 a barrel with a median near $8. On an EIA spot basis, it averaged $68 in September, the richest month since 2006, and even after the sharp drop to the low $40s, it remains well above average. In other words, spreads have plenty of room to decline as refiners still have the financial incentive to produce as much gasoline and diesel as possible.

Gasoline remains more than a dollar above year-ago levels, so annual price comparisons will likely remain inflationary until spring. However, the Fed Funds futures markets are pricing roughly 75 basis points of further tightening. Hiking into falling energy prices looks to us like the Fed is fighting yesterday’s war.

Market Trading Update

Yesterday, we compared Nvidia’s earnings risk to the “safety” premium investors pay for Walmart. Today, I want to return to the Santa Claus rally we discussed in Tuesday’s commentary, but from a different angle. The question isn’t whether it shows up. It’s WHEN.

Goldman’s flow desk made a sharp point this week. Two-month seasonal averages are too blunt for this tape. Their S&P 500 path, going back to 1928, shows a Thanksgiving ramp, a stall in early December, and a second-leg higher. Read off their chart, roughly 80% of the average gain arrives after December 14. We ran the same test on S&P 500 total returns since 2003, and the shape holds.

The sequence makes sense once you look at who is trading. Retail buying and corporate buybacks typically carry stocks into early December. Then the plumbing gets in the way. Many mutual funds set capital gains distribution record dates around the second week of December, and some taxable investors sell ahead of them to dodge the bill. Tax-loss selling peaks. Goldman expects the buyback window to close around December 13, the Fed meets December 8 and 9, and December 18 brings quarterly options expiration. Once that pile-up clears, managers dress up their books for year-end reporting, and the Santa Claus rally gets its second wind.

Here’s where it gets interesting. Since 2010, the December 5 to 14 window has lost 0.27% on average and finished higher in only 7 of 16 years. In most years, it’s a pause. In 2011, 2014, 2015, and 2018, it was a 3%-3.6% hit.

Goldman’s base rates for years like this one, when the VIX starts mid-November at 18 or higher, deserve respect. The median drawdown inside the window was 3%, and the year-end gain averaged just 1.34%. With the S&P 500 closing Wednesday near 7,318, about 6% below its October 6 record, we’re already living part of that script.

We should not dismiss that hedge funds and CTAs are very underweight technology stocks, which does provide a potential tailwind. However, there is always the risk that they choose to remain sidelined through year-end.

Here is how to play the next few weeks.

  • First, don’t chase the Thanksgiving pop. If the ramp shows up, use strength into early December to trim winners back to target weight and rebuild cash.

  • Secondly, put that cash to work into mid-December weakness, ahead of the stretch that historically does the heavy lifting.

That’s the playbook in our Equity Conservative Growth and Equity Aggressive Growth models. The calendar rewards patience, not urgency. Such is the nature of seasonal trading.

Santa usually shows up, but if you lose too much before then, the gift of Christmas doesn’t really matter.

Fed Worries About AI Financing Web

The October FOMC minutes, released yesterday, contain a passage worth focusing on. Per the minutes, most participants “observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly,” and much of that growth “had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures.”

A few participants noted that AI exposures were “becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms.” They also flagged off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing among AI firms as potential loss amplifiers.

We wrote about this last week in Nvidia Circular Financing: Who Is At Risk?, where we traced the guarantees, residual value support, and off-balance-sheet lease backstops that Nvidia was providing to support the AI buildout and, in turn, chip purchases. Our conclusion was that the companies most at risk were those like CoreWeave, with high interest rates and seemingly losing access to the capital markets. The Fed agrees.

Here is why this mention in the minutes is important. The Fed does not casually put a sector’s financing structure into its minutes. Describing AI debt as opaque and concentrated moves it from market chatter to a documented financial stability concern, and that may be the first step toward supervisory attention.

The tension between Fed policy and the AI debt is worth appreciating. In the minutes, almost all participants judged that “further action to raise the target range” would “likely be appropriate,” and two members suggested, “an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting.” The Fed is now identifying a leveraged, opaque, and concentrated credit structure while preparing to raise its cost of funding. We will watch credit spreads, not equity prices, for any potential fallout. The graphic below is courtesy of The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: The Nvidia Story: Three Assessments Intersected
data.description:
Let’s pick up where we ended last week, when the details about Jensen Huang’s affairs and his subsequent ousting at Nvidia (NVDA) were just coming out.

Considering all that has happened in the intervening days, we need to go much deeper. This is one of the most important geopolitical developments of this year—and if it leads to a material and imminent worsening in US-China relations, one could make the argument that it is the most important development of the year.

THE SITUATION

Jensen Huang’s travails intersect three major geopolitical assessments I hold.

The first, which has received fair pushback from readers, is the long-term rivalry that is emerging between sovereign states and powerful tech companies. I argue that the Mag 7 and other tech companies that shape our daily lives are fundamentally expressions of a unipolar world. The worldview of these companies is ’90s-esque in their unbridled optimism and self-confidence in their mission. They see themselves as transcending politics because, in the ’90s, politics had been transcended. Communism lost, liberal democracy won, so let’s beat our missiles into iPhones and make memes.

The second is that the US-China relationship is on a trajectory of eventual conflict. If there is any bias in my work, it is that I think an eventual war between the US and China would be very bad for the world, for the US, and for China. I hope it doesn’t come to that. Hope isn’t analysis, however, and Washington and Beijing have fundamentally incoherent geopolitical imperatives. The US seeks to maintain its global primacy. China is not willing to kowtow and believes, at minimum, it should enjoy regional primacy. Yes, the US and Chinese economies are deeply interconnected. So were European economies on the eve of World War I. Graham Allison studied 16 historical cases of a rising power threatening to displace an established one; 12 ended in war.

The third is that the next two years will be relatively stable in US-China relations. Say what you will about President Donald Trump; he does not accept that the US and China should be rivals. He has worked hard to forge a constructive relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping. I have gone so far as to tell my clients to enjoy the next two years as the most stable in the US-China relationship we’ll see in the next 10.

The Nvidia story is a powerful confirmatory signal for assessments one and two. It is profoundly contradictory for the third.

1. The Jack Ma Parallel

What is happening to Jensen Huang and Nvidia is not much different than what happened to Chinese tech mogul Jack Ma and Alibaba back in 2020.

In October 2020, on the eve of an IPO for his fintech company Ant Group, Jack Ma went on stage in Shanghai and sharply criticized China’s banking system and government. Within two weeks, he’d been summoned for “regulatory talks” and his IPO was suspended. Months later, the Chinese government called China’s major tech companies’ leaders into a single room and told them essentially that unless they wanted to have the Jack Ma experience, they would do as the CPC—and specifically as Xi Jinping—said. China subsequently acquired shares with board seats in some of these companies, including Alibaba (BABA), and told them where they’d be allowed to sell, emphasizing the Chinese domestic market as their “mainstay.”

Is this really that different than the US government acquiring shares in companies it deems critical to its national security? In August 2025, Nvidia and AMD (AMD) agreed to pay the US government 15% of their revenue from Chinese sales of H20 AI chips and MI308 chips in exchange for export licenses. Jensen Huang is in trouble in part because he did not want to abide by US export controls (i.e., restrictions on where Nvidia would be allowed to sell its products). The only real difference is that in China, Jack Ma and others got on the wrong side of Xi Jinping; in the US, Jensen assumed a good relationship with President Trump would protect him. It did until the midterms, but now President Trump is weak, and the sharks smell blood in the water.

This is the beginning of a US government crackdown on tech. The state, to paraphrase Max Weber, is the monopoly on the legitimate use of force within given borders. The White House controls the men with guns. The men with data, capital, and technology possess extraordinary powers, but they must bend to the will of the men with guns.

2. The Next Boogeyman

The US has always needed boogeymen to define itself against—the British, the “Yellow Peril,” Japan, Nazi Germany, the Soviet Union. China is the next country on this list. It is also the first time in US history that its chosen rival is bigger. China lacks many things, to be sure. It cannot feed its own population, and it has grown dependent on energy imports. But at a very simple level, China has more people than the US. Neither the Soviet Union nor the combined forces of Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan could compete with the US on a demographic level.

They also could not compete with US manufacturing prowess. The US produced more merchant shipping tonnage in a single year than Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan produced in all of World War II combined. China is the world’s factory now; it accounts for 28–35% of global manufacturing output depending on your definition, and without Chinese rare earths and magnets and other components, the US economy will not work. The US is actively derisking its dependence on China, but this is a process that will take several years, if not decades. And the inconvenient truth is that today, the US is no less dependent on Chinese manufacturing than China is on access to Western markets and capital. This dependence only deepens US paranoia and drives it to manipulate markets away from China.

For most of its long history, China was content to be a dominant economic power within its own sphere of influence. But the growth of the Chinese population and the globalization of supply chains means that China is now dependent on trade and global supply chains. This is not your ancestors’ Middle Kingdom. This is a modern industrial state that must build a blue-water navy to defend its supply lines from enemies, whether pirates or US destroyers. In other words, China cannot defend its national security without creating the kind of military capabilities that Washington will interpret as a direct threat to its own primacy.

At a certain point, it is academic to argue whether China intends to pursue expansionist aims. Unless the CPC implodes (possible, if unlikely), the US and China will increasingly compete with and be suspicious of each other.

3. The Next Two Years

For all his talk of Make America Great Again, President Trump does not hold a fundamentalist belief in American primacy. President Trump has openly called the US-China relationship “the G2.” He sees China as a peer power with which he can make a deal. All his tariffs and machismo and posturing is about creating leverage to make a deal with China—not to fight China or assert US primacy.

Elements of President Trump’s own cabinet are not with him on this. Secretary of State and National Security Advisor Marco Rubio is a well-known China hawk and likely the source of the Jensen leaks. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has openly criticized Nvidia and China policy.

Moreover, being anti-China is one of the few true bipartisan positions left, and the Democrats seem to be relishing the Nvidia scandal for generating opportunities for hearings, aka political theater.

All of which leads me to the conclusion that my optimism about the next two years in the US-China relationship is broken. So far, what we’ve seen after the midterms:

  • Stephen Miller (as hardline a cabinet official as there is on China) elevated to Chief of Staff

  • Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent effectively kneecapping Trump’s friend Jensen Huang and his company Nvidia without so much as a peep from the president

  • In recent weeks, a steady drumbeat of quotes from officials like Bessent and US Trade Rep Jamieson Greer on China not living up to its prior trade and economic commitments.

We’ll see if President Trump is able to right things in his upcoming meeting with Xi—if he uses these developments to extract more concessions as part of his dealmaking tactics, or if he uses the China cudgel to his own benefit to buttress his abysmally low approval ratings. After all, he used anti-China invective to great effect in his first campaign back in 2015/2016. Time for some reruns.

Am I making a mountain out of a molehill? Perhaps we will know soon. But as George Friedman once told me, “Get excited, then get smart.” If you wait until something is obvious, you will always be behind. The only way to catch the one development in 10 that matters is to get excited about all 10, including the nine that end up not mattering. On this one, I’m excited.

MAP/CHART OF THE WEEK

BLIND SPOT

It has been a rough few weeks for Indonesia. The rupiah has fallen to record lows on the dollar. MSCI warned last month that the country’s emerging-market status was in jeopardy, leading to the benchmark Jakarta index tumbling ~15% (from which it still has not recovered). Last week, Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka—son of former President Joko Widodo (aka Jokowi)—resigned after questions about his educational credentials led to threats of impeachment.

Gibran’s joining the ticket with current Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto was seen as a positive note of stability in the country’s politics, but that is gone now. Prabowo is instead consolidating power, removing Jokowi allies from positions of power. Prabowo’s tenure has seen attacks on central bank independence, turmoil in the finance ministry, off-budget populist spending programs, and doubts about the governance of the country’s new sovereign wealth fund. Widespread Gen-Z/student protests erupted in August and September over inflation and governance issues but have fizzled (for now).

Indonesia is the fourth most populous nation in the world at ~300 million people. Its demographics are (relatively) strong. It is the world’s most populous Muslim-majority nation, and its relationship with Islam is famously moderate and pluralistic. The country sits astride critical maritime trade corridors. It contains impressive reserves of critical resources like nickel and copper, and is a major coal producer. In a multipolar world, Indonesia should be a rising power.

And yet the country seems determined to squander its potential. Some of this is understandable—Indonesia is a unique archipelagic nation, home to many different ethnic groups and languages. But Jokowi’s presidency seemed to be a break from the past, suggesting to optimistic observers that Indonesia might be on the cusp of transcending its differences, of utilizing its diversity as a strength rather than as something that was holding it back. But it turns out Prabowo, who has deep family ties to the authoritarian regime of Suharto and lived in self-imposed exile for years due to allegations over his role in the kidnapping and torture of pro-democracy activists, is reverting to form, attempting to centralize power rather than build coalitions.

data.title: Heavy Selling Is Clustering - What To Expect Next
data.description:
Market Breadth Watch: Heavy Selling Is Clustering: What To Expect Next

Two volume readings flashed the same message this week.

Two different volume readings flashed the same message this week: the selling is coming in clusters, not single days. One measures the whole NYSE, the other SPY’s own trading. Below is what each one shows and what SPY did after similar stretches before.

1. NYSE down volume: four heavy days in six sessions

On Thursday (Nov 19), 86% of NYSE volume went into falling stocks and 82% of issues declined. On its own that is a heavy day, not a rare one. What stands out is the clustering: it was the fourth day of 78% or more NYSE down volume in the last six sessions (Nov 12: 80%, Nov 16: 78%, Nov 17: 79%, Nov 19: 86%).

What SPY did after heavy NYSE selling, 1998 to 2026

2. SPY’s own volume: three heavy down days in four sessions

SPY fell 2.0% on Thursday to $715.87 on 76 million shares, 1.65 times its 50-day average. It was the third down day in four sessions with volume at 1.5 times the average or more (Nov 16: 1.54x, Nov 17: 1.57x, Nov 19: 1.65x).

SPY’s volume shows three such clusters since June. In June, SPY made its low (about 725) inside the cluster and rallied to 778 by early August. The Oct 30 to Nov 5 cluster included the biggest volume day of the period (126 million shares, 3 times the average) and was followed by a bounce to 760. This one is different: all three heavy days are down days, and SPY is at a new low for the period with no bounce yet.

What SPY did after its own heavy-volume selling, 1993 to 2026

What stands out

Both say the same thing

Whether you count heavy selling across the NYSE or in SPY itself, a cluster of heavy days was followed by better-than-normal returns: about twice the normal 20-day gain and better odds. Repeated selling tends to use up the sellers.

More selling usually comes first

After an 85%+ NYSE down-volume day, another one followed within 10 sessions more than half the time (106 of 189), and the median low over the next 20 days was 1.9% below that day’s close. In SPY’s own clusters the median case also saw a close 2.4% lower within 20 days. Feb 25, 2020 was one of those cases, and it came before the worst of that crash.

Not a guaranteed low

The edge shows up over one to three months, not in a straight line. The fall of 2023 had a similar stretch: after the third heavy NYSE day (Oct 3), more heavy days followed and SPY fell another 2.6% over three weeks before the low on Oct 27.

What to watch

An up day on heavy volume

In SPY, a heavy-volume up day would be the first sign the selling is being absorbed, as on Jun 11 and Nov 4. More heavy down days at lower closes would mean the cluster is still building.

The oversold gauge turning up inside the cluster

The oversold gauge I track is deep in its low zone, in the lowest 1.3% of all readings since 2004. Its strongest buy signal in back-tests is the day its slower reading turns back up from oversold, and that has not happened yet.

When the turn came during an NYSE selling cluster (three or more days of 78%+ NYSE down volume within six sessions), SPY was higher 20 days later in 22 of 25 cases since 2007, by about 5% on average (3.7% without the 2009 and 2020 rebounds), against about 3% for the turn on its own. The misses were Oct 2008 (-8.6%), Jun 2010 (-2.0%) and Oct 2023 (-0.5%). 25 cases is a small sample, so I treat it as a confirmation, not a system.

Timing matters

The six-session window moves forward each day and older heavy days drop out of it. With Nov 16, 17, and 19 in the window, a turn on Friday (Nov 20) or Monday (Nov 23) would still count. From Tuesday on it needs fresh 78%+ days to keep the cluster alive.

data.title: TradingView MCP: When Artificial Intelligence Got Its Hands On The Pine Script Compiler
data.description:
A few years ago, developing a trading strategy began with learning a programming language. Then came large language models, and traders could describe their ideas in plain English. There was, however, considerable distance between receiving a piece of source code and having a working strategy. The AI wrote the program, the trader copied it into Pine Editor, the compiler complained, and the trader went back to the AI. Sometimes this exchange of pleasantries lasted longer than the development of the trading idea itself.

On November 16, 2026, TradingView gave AI agents access to its native Pine Script compiler and strategy backtesting engine through its own MCP server. Against the relentless stream of artificial intelligence announcements, the news could easily go unnoticed. Yet for the algorithmic trading industry, it may prove considerably more significant than the arrival of another language model.

TradingView has reduced the need for a human intermediary between artificial intelligence and the development environment.

A Compiler at the Other End of the Conversation

The Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open standard that allows AI applications to interact with external software. In TradingView's case, the agent communicates with the same computational infrastructure that powers the platform itself.

The language model can now receive feedback directly from the compiler, including line numbers, error positions and warnings. It can correct a program, validate it again and run it against historical market data.

TradingView has introduced eight tools for working with Pine Script:

  • validate_pine_script — validates source code.

  • run_pine_indicator — calculates indicator values.

  • run_pine_backtest — runs a trading strategy backtest.

  • get_pine_script_source — retrieves accessible source code.

  • get_pine_script_info — retrieves script parameters and output information.

  • search_pine_scripts — searches for scripts.

  • create_pine_script and update_pine_script — create and update scripts within the user's account.

When a program is updated, TradingView preserves its previous versions, while code that fails compilation is not saved to the account. Intermediate experiments can be conducted without saving the source code. Other authors' protected and invite-only publications remain inaccessible.

What is particularly noteworthy is that TradingView has not built a separate development environment for artificial intelligence. Instead, it has opened the existing infrastructure that Pine Script developers have been using for years.

Connecting TradingView to Artificial Intelligence

The official MCP server is available here.

The connection uses Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1 authorization. TradingView supports ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, Cursor and other compatible applications. Users simply add the appropriate connector and authorize access through their TradingView account. Detailed instructions are available in the official MCP documentation.

While preparing this article, I connected TradingView to ChatGPT and tried the new integration while developing a strategy based on liquidity sweeps and false breakouts. The purpose was to see how much of the development and testing process could be delegated to the AI agent. The trading idea did not automatically become profitable, but the need to constantly transfer code and test results between applications was considerably reduced. The first noticeable restriction was the number of available requests.

For developers accustomed to working with Pine Editor and Strategy Tester, this way of interacting with the platform may initially feel unfamiliar. After a few iterations, however, it becomes apparent how much time was previously spent on tasks that required neither market knowledge nor any particular programming talent.

Backtesting Is No Longer a Manual Exercise

Throughout the history of financial technology, the cost of computation has repeatedly determined who could afford to employ particular methods of market research. Computing power once reserved for large banks and investment firms gradually found its way onto the retail trader's desk. Now the distance between a trading hypothesis and its computational investigation is shrinking as well.

Through MCP, artificial intelligence can access Strategy Tester statistics: net profit, profit factor, maximum drawdown, total trades, percentage of profitable positions, average profits and losses, and Sharpe and Sortino ratios. The agent can examine individual trades and compare the performance of long and short positions. With an eligible subscription, Deep Backtesting allows research over a specified historical period.

The investigation of a trading system rarely ends with its first successful backtest. It remains necessary to determine how much the results depend on the instrument, timeframe, indicator parameters and prevailing market conditions. Sometimes changing a single number is enough to make a splendid set of statistics disappear.

Until now, such work required considerable involvement from the developer. A sequence of experiments can increasingly be delegated to an AI agent, leaving the human responsible for defining the research question and interpreting the results.

An equally important change concerns the quality of the software itself. One longstanding criticism of language models is their ability to produce entirely nonfunctional programs with disarming confidence. Access to the compiler and execution results makes it possible to uncover many of these mistakes during development. It also becomes easier to establish whether correcting one part of a strategy has inadvertently damaged another.

The quality of AI-assisted software development will improve not only because language models are becoming more capable, but because their mistakes are becoming easier to expose.

There is, of course, another side to this development. Curve-fitting trading strategies to historical data existed long before artificial intelligence. MCP could turn it into an industrial operation. An agent instructed to maximize profitability may discover a magnificent combination of parameters that proves entirely useless outside the period under investigation.

The market is under no obligation to repeat history simply because a computer has learned to study it faster.

Ten Calls Before Breakfast

Beginning November 17, 2026, TradingView applies the following daily MCP usage limits:

The additional AI subscription also carries a limit of 50 requests per minute. Usage limits reflect TradingView’s documentation at publication and may change.

These figures deserve some attention. A single question put to an AI assistant may require several calls to TradingView. Compiling a program, running a backtest, validating a correction and saving a script are separate operations, each consuming part of the overall allowance.

Ten requests may seem perfectly adequate to an occasional chatbot user. A trading system developer could exhaust them before breakfast.

Having removed a human bottleneck from Pine Script development, TradingView has introduced a computational one. The availability of a paid AI subscription also reveals the commercial logic of the arrangement. The company can now sell not only access to analytical tools, but additional computational capacity for artificial intelligence.

In the coming years, the cost of a research iteration may become a factor in its own right when choosing a trading platform.

MetaTrader Is Keeping Pace

TradingView is hardly alone in this endeavor. On July 23, 2026, MetaQuotes introduced MetaTrader 5 Build 6060, with native support for MCP and agentic artificial intelligence. The integration extends across the trading terminal and MetaEditor, allowing AI agents to work with MQL5 source code, compile programs, and test and optimize Expert Advisors. Further details are available in the MetaEditor MCP and AI documentation. Unlike TradingView, MetaTrader's implementation also extends to trading operations. Within four months, two of the largest ecosystems in retail algorithmic trading have given artificial intelligence direct access to development tools previously operated by humans. That is hardly a coincidence.

From Source Code to an Actual Trade

TradingView has drawn a fairly clear distinction between strategy research and trade execution. Its MCP terms of use prohibit using the server for automated trading, trading decisions or connections to trading bots.

For the execution of separately developed and tested strategies, the established mechanism remains trading alerts and webhooks. A Pine Script signal is passed to external software that communicates with a trading platform or broker. This is a separate workflow, not permission to connect TradingView’s MCP server or its alerts to automated trading systems.

As the development of trading algorithms becomes more accessible, demand for execution infrastructure is likely to grow as well. Broker restrictions, position sizing, duplicate signal handling and discrepancies between simulated and actual execution will remain very much a part of the business.

Artificial intelligence considerably simplifies the development of a trading system, but the financial responsibility for its operation still rests with the owner of the trading account.

Storm Clouds Over Alternative Compilers

TradingView's November announcement arrives at a rather inconvenient moment for several young projects born out of Pine Script's limitations. PyneCore and PyneComp offer a route for bringing trading algorithms into Python, while PineForge translates Pine Script v6 into C++ and provides its own backtesting engine, accessible through MCP. PyneCore's developers report compatibility testing across 1,000 published TradingView scripts, while PineForge presents results from nearly 8,000 backtests. These are the projects' own published findings, not independent assessments of their compatibility with the original.

The engineering value of these developments cannot be dismissed. Independent execution, proprietary market datasets and large-scale testing remain attractive propositions, particularly in light of TradingView's daily quotas. Yet as recently as last week, the ability to backtest Pine Script from an AI client without human intervention looked like a substantial competitive advantage. Now the owner of the language itself provides access to the original compiler, historical market data and its native execution environment. Selling independence from TradingView may remain a profitable business. Selling an alternative to its compiler solely for the convenience of AI-assisted development will become considerably harder. Storm clouds are gathering over this young market, and, ironically enough, they have come from TradingView's own cloud infrastructure.

Disclosure: The author uses TradingView as a software platform but has no commercial relationship, sponsorship, partnership or compensation arrangement with TradingView, MetaQuotes, PyneCore, PyneComp or PineForge. This article is neither sponsored nor promotional. No compensation has been received for covering any of the companies or projects mentioned. All references and external links are provided solely for readers' convenience and independent research.

A credit bubble of immense and dangerous proportions.

I immediately dubbed it Armageddon ’08 in the then brand spanking new NFTRH because that is what it was, a final reckoning of good (natural market functioning) vs. evil (remote controlled markets managed by monetary socialists in favor of the financial services industry).

In today’s reckoning, ‘good’ seeks not to unwind commercial credit but instead, official (government/Fed) credit and debt. The kind of $40T plus in leverage that has maintained a rising GDP but and even better rising Debt-to-GDP.

At 121% debt leverage, the word “unsustainable” is way too mild. This train must be stopped!

However, that potential benefit did not provide immediate support for the stock on Thursday.

Nvidia has been under pressure as investors reassess the sustainability of the AI investment cycle.

The stock has fallen 38% since reaching a record closing high of $239.24 on October 6, as concerns about infrastructure spending and financing requirements have weighed on sentiment.

The company also faces uncertainty following Huang's resignation last week.

Reports concerning allegations involving the former CEO and a woman accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset have added to the negative sentiment surrounding the chipmaker.

data.title: Wall Street Chokes On Anthropic As The AI Trade Comes Unstuck
data.description:
The liquidity arithmetic was hard to ignore. Anthropic (ANT) raised $81.3 billion through its public offering, or $107.3 billion including the $26 billion strategic private placement, while the S&P 500 shed approximately $1.3 trillion in market value during the session. Those numbers aren’t directly comparable, and they certainly don’t establish that IPO funding caused the equity losses. But they capture the uncomfortable optics of a market trying to absorb an enormous new asset while everything surrounding it was being marked down.

Takeaways by Dark Side of the Boom

• The biggest IPO in history delivered a spectacular opening, but Wall Street couldn’t swallow the supply without choking on the rest of the market.

• Anthropic’s success exposed an increasingly uncomfortable divide between investors willing to pay for frontier AI and those still financing the infrastructure beneath it.

• A heavily short gamma market turned an ordinary sell the news reversal into a disorderly liquidation, with options hedging pouring fuel on the fire.

• King Dollar and Treasuries found buyers as equities, precious metals and crypto buckled, leaving Friday’s options expiration as the next potential turning point.

Wall Street Chokes on Anthropic

Wall Street rolled out the red carpet for Anthropic, uncorked the champagne and promptly gagged on the biggest IPO in history. What began as a celebration of artificial intelligence ended with the S&P 500 down 2%, the Nasdaq swinging from gains of more than 2% to losses of roughly the same magnitude, and more than 460 members of the benchmark retreating. The S&P has now fallen for six consecutive sessions, its longest losing streak since April 2024, while the Dow is knocking on the door of a technical correction. For a market supposedly desperate to rediscover its AI mojo, this was an extraordinarily expensive way to demonstrate enthusiasm.

Some context: the S&P 500 lost around $1.3 trillion in market cap today as Anthropic's IPO went out around $1.3 trillion.

Anthropic itself wasn’t the problem, at least not in the conventional sense. The stock opened at $111.50 against its $83 IPO price, an immediate premium of more than 34%, before sellers descended and whittled the advance to roughly 17% by the close. That still leaves the Claude developer with a fully diluted valuation approaching $1.8 trillion, putting it among the ten largest public companies on the planet. The IPO was a triumph for the underwriters and early shareholders. Unfortunately, the rest of Wall Street appeared to have been invited to the party mainly to pick up the bill.

The timing was almost comical. Equity futures rallied overnight on expectations that Anthropic would restore confidence in the AI complex, only for the broader market to begin losing altitude as the opening indication for ANT climbed. Then came reports that many institutional investors had received little or no allocation. Whether that reflected overwhelming demand or an unusually concentrated distribution, it left the market trying to price a record offering against a backdrop of increasingly fragile risk appetite.

And once ANT began trading around midday, the wheels really came off.

The Biggest IPO Meets Wall Street’s Worst Positioning

The problem wasn’t simply that investors decided to sell the news. The market was carrying a particularly nasty options configuration into the session, with dealers reportedly holding their largest short gamma exposure since 2019. Nomura’s Charlie McElligott had already flagged the dangerous collision between Nvidia, Anthropic and November options expiration, and Thursday delivered the sort of violent price action that makes dealers wish they’d taken the afternoon off.

Short gamma doesn’t tell you which direction the market will travel. It tells you how quickly things can get ugly once it chooses one. When dealers are short gamma, their hedging tends to reinforce the prevailing move, buying into rallies and selling into declines. Had the opening enthusiasm survived, the same machinery could have helped launch a spectacular squeeze. Instead, equities rolled over, zero-day options activity amplified the afternoon decline, and the hedging machinery began feeding the very weakness it was supposed to manage.

There was plenty of dry tinder. Goldman’s prime brokerage data showed hedge funds carrying technology exposure of roughly 18% against an index weight near 29%, an extraordinary 11-percentage-point underweight. On paper, that left enormous room for a rally if investors were forced to chase performance. But underweight investors aren’t necessarily eager buyers when the market starts falling through the floor. The hoped-for squeeze never arrived, leaving sellers with precious little resistance.

The damage spread well beyond the obvious AI names. The Magnificent Seven surrendered their early gains, neocloud stocks went from roughly 6% higher to 4% lower, and all eleven S&P sectors finished in the red. The VIX approached 28, volatility of volatility climbed above 125, and rising implied correlation suggested that investors were no longer distinguishing much between winners and losers. The market was selling risk rather than carefully selecting casualties.

And the liquidity arithmetic was hard to ignore. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion through its public offering, or $107.3 billion including the $26 billion strategic private placement, while the S&P 500 shed approximately $1.3 trillion in market value during the session. Those numbers aren’t directly comparable, and they certainly don’t establish that IPO funding caused the equity losses. But they capture the uncomfortable optics of a market trying to absorb an enormous new asset while everything surrounding it was being marked down.

The money had to come from somewhere. And judging by the performance of Nvidia (NVDA), copper, gold, and crypto, investors weren’t exactly reaching into their spare-change jars.

The AI Winner Takes the Money, but the Builders Take the Beating

The more revealing fault line is emerging between the businesses developing frontier AI models and the sprawling infrastructure trade that finances their ambitions.

Anthropic’s debut demonstrates that investors remain willing to pay extraordinary prices for a leading model developer. What it doesn’t establish is that the market has rediscovered an unlimited appetite for debt-heavy cloud operators, semiconductor suppliers and the financing arrangements supporting the AI construction boom.

That’s a much tougher proposition, especially as interest rates climb and credit investors become more discriminating.

AMD (AMD) was caught in a separate storm after Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position and raised allegations involving China-related risks and financing arrangements. AMD denied wrongdoing, but the stock was hammered nonetheless. New US chip licensing restrictions also pressured Taiwan Semiconductor-exposed companies and Asian data-centre names, adding another layer of uncertainty to an industry already struggling to defend its capital spending assumptions.

Credit markets reflected the broader discomfort. Investment-grade and high-yield spreads swung sharply before finishing wider across sectors, although hyperscaler and data-centre credit held up somewhat better than the equity carnage might suggest.

The distinction between buying a successful AI model developer and underwriting the entire infrastructure race is becoming increasingly important. Anthropic can attract a mountain of equity capital without proving that every supplier, neocloud operator and leveraged data-centre project deserves its previous valuation.

Wall Street appears increasingly willing to finance the perceived winners while demanding a much harder reckoning from everyone selling them the shovels.

Meanwhile, the dollar and Treasuries offered the usual escape routes from a badly bruised equity market. The ten-year Treasury yield drifted back toward 5%, even as crude oil edged higher following renewed attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz. The historic Trump-Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen produced a declaration supporting increased refined petroleum supply, but the oil market appeared more interested in physical security than diplomatic choreography.

King Dollar extended its advance to seven of the past eight sessions, reaching fresh 18-month highs as high-beta currencies came under pressure. The Colombian peso and offshore yuan were among the casualties of a broader carry unwind, while gold slipped below $3,700 for the first time since September 2025. Bitcoin (BTC.X) suffered another ugly round trip, retreating toward its July lows.

When bonds and the dollar are attracting money while gold, crypto and equities are being liquidated together, the market is telling you that immediate liquidity has become more valuable than long-term investment narratives.

And that’s where Friday’s options expiration becomes particularly important.

The S&P 500 has now slipped further below its 200-day moving average (nothing good happens when any asset slips below the 200-day Dark Side of the Boom), with the sixth consecutive decline adding an uncomfortable technical dimension to the fundamental debate.

Historical comparisons offer some consolation: on the three previous occasions over the past 30 years when the index posted six straight declines while finishing less than 3% below its 200-day average, equities were higher five sessions later. Unfortunately, each episode was followed by more substantial downside.

With the S&P’s intraday low near 7,193, the 7,000–7,100 area being watched by technical traders is beginning to look considerably less remote.

Friday’s expiration could release some of the negative gamma that helped turn Thursday’s reversal into a rout, potentially allowing the market to stabilise heading toward Thanksgiving. But that would resolve a mechanical pressure point, not the wider argument about AI profitability, borrowing costs and the increasingly selective appetite for technology risk.

Anthropic’s first session proved that Wall Street still has an enormous appetite for the AI crown jewels. The trouble is that investors seem increasingly willing to sell the rest of the kingdom to pay for them. And after Thursday’s spectacular failure to sustain an opening rally, I’d be watching what happens to Nvidia and the broader technology complex after the options machinery resets, rather than taking comfort from another impressive print in ANT.

The board of Paytm Singapore Pte Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of One 97 Communications, approved the investment and partnership with Funding Asia Group Pte Ltd, which operates as Funding Societies.

Under this arrangement, Paytm will provide payments and lending technology to help CardUp expand its financial services business in Singapore. In return, Paytm will earn technology fees and a share of the revenue. The agreement will initially remain valid for five years and may be renewed if both parties agree.

The company said the move is part of its plan to expand into selected international markets through a partnership-based business model. Under this model, Paytm will provide its payment technology platform and devices, while its local partners will handle sales, distribution and daily operations. Paytm aims to earn revenue through licensing fees, revenue sharing and other arrangements while keeping its investment relatively limited.

CardUp, which was established in Singapore in 2015, operates in the digital payments business. Its revenue increased to Rs 2,992 million in 2025, compared with Rs 1,943.8 million in 2024 and Rs 1,041.6 million in 2023.

Funding Societies, a digital financing platform that provides loans and financial services to small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs), acquired CardUp in 2024 for an undisclosed amount.

data.title: Dow Industrial Average Takes Biggest Hit As Bitcoin Struggles
data.description:
Another day of selling swept the market which left many indices trading below their 200-day MAs. This is good for long term investors as it resets the pullback count which will create the next big buying opportunity. On the downside, it's all painful to watch.

The Dow Industrial Average had been performing well, at least until today. There was a clear slice of the June swing low, and loss of 50K support, with technicals now net negative. I had market two measured move targets; the first was cleanly sliced, the second has almost been reached. The worry is that this is just the start of the selling. For better (or worse), trading volume was light.

The bigger surprise was the damage done in Bitcoin (BTC.X). This was an asset that originally sold hard into the July low, before it found some demand. But now it finds itself struggling to hold current support. Last week's spike low (from the bullish hammer) is set to be negated as a reversal candlestick, but there is an aggressive buy with a very tight stop (loss of $62K) as I have seen recoveries from similar situations in the past. But this is crash territory and there isn't a whole lot of support below $57.5K

The S&P loss 7,250 support as part of the 200-day MA undercut. Technicals are net negative and oversold. There is still a chance for a 'bear' trap, but as other indices move away from support it becomes harder to see this leading a recovery, but that shouldn't discount the possibility; a move above 7.25K would confirm a 'bear trap'.

It's not all doom-and-gloom. The equal-weighted S&P took a big hit, but it's still range bound, so losses remain noise within the larger trading range. Technicals are net negative but it hasn't yet challenged its 200-day MA or range support, so if the index can hold on it may yet take on a leadership role on the next recovery.

The Russell 2000 (IWM) finally gave up October swing low support. Remember, triple tops or bottoms are rare, so if an asset touches a support or resistance level for a third time then the chance for a break is high. Technicals are net bearish and oversold, so this is crash territory. As an added point, watch for a bearish 'Death Cross' between 50-day and 200-day MA which extends the decline to something more long term.

The Nasdaq, like Bitcoin, closed with a bearish engulfing pattern that has challenged the spike low from the bullish hammer earlier this week. Technicals are net bearish and primed for a crash.

Ironically, Semiconductors (SOX) had a relatively quiet day. Today marked a bearish engulfing pattern, but as this an index in an oversold state there is no additional bearish weight to this pattern; it's a reversal pattern, not a continuation one.

With losses of 200-day MAs the indices are no longer at a quick bounce, so now it's a best case for a sideways move rather than further losses. Personally, I would like to see a buying opportunity similar to what we saw in April 2025 as I have money to put to work...

data.title: Indian Rupee Rallies Further Amid FIIs Buying Spree

During the day, the USD/INR pair posts a fresh seven-month low marginally below 93.00.

On Thursday, Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) remain net buyers in the Indian stock market again and raised their stake in equities worth Rs. 7,411.41 crore. So far in November, FIIs has made investments worth Rs. 1,01,640.97 crore.

What has improved India’s appeal in recent weeks?

According to The Economic Times (ET), India has been described as an “anti-AI” trade because it was left out of much of the global AI rally and has limited direct exposure to the AI supply chain. Any unwinding of crowded AI-linked positions could therefore encourage investors to rotate into other emerging markets, including India and Brazil.

Analysts at DBS said in a note that “regional equity plays that have been relatively less exposed to the AI-play this year appear to be benefiting in the initial phase of re-allocation”.

Strategists at Danske Bank highlight that the recent sell-off in crude has been substantial, with “oil prices… down around 20% this month,” as the market responds to “recovering supply from the Middle East” and growing “expectations that US President Donald Trump will avoid renewed full-scale hostilities with Iran.”

Investors shrug off rally in US Dollar

Technical Analysis: USD/INR sees more downside towards 92.50

In the daily chart, USD/INR trades at 93.00, extending its decline below the short-term trend as the 20-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) at 94.11 now caps the upside. The pair retains a bearish near-term bias while it holds under this dynamic resistance, although the Relative Strength Index (RSI) at 24.83 shows oversold conditions that hint at the risk of a corrective bounce rather than a clean trend acceleration lower.

On the topside, initial resistance is located at the 20-day EMA around 94.11, and a daily close above this barrier would be needed to ease immediate downside pressure and open room for a broader recovery. On the downside, the pair could extend its decline towards 92.44.
